title: Darcy Graham lifts lid on injury and why he's 'glad' he made decision he did
article_text:
Darcy Graham acknowledged he could easily have been looking in from the outside instead of basking in the after-glow of his fifth Scotland hat-trick.

Edinburgh head coach Sean Everitt revealed in September that the prolific wing was set to be out until Christmas with a bicep problem sustained in a pre-season friendly.

But a few weeks later it emerged that Graham and his club had opted to go down the rehabilitation route rather than surgery, and the 29-year-old was able to return to action last month, paving the way for him to be involved in Gregor Townsend’s Nations Championship squad.

After playing his part in last weekend’s hard-fought 15-12 win over Australia, Graham notched a treble in Saturday’s 67-5 rout of Japan, taking his tally for Scotland to 41 tries and moving him six clear of clubmate Duhan van der Merwe at the top of the national team’s all-time scoring charts.

“I actually said to the physio before the game I’m glad we went the non-surgical route on that bicep, as I wouldn’t have been here (otherwise), I would have been out until Christmas time,” Graham said.

“That Glasgow game (on December 27) was my return to play, so my season could have looked very different.

“If you can keep away from the operation table, it’s definitely better to do that. We had that two-week period to try and see how my arm coped with training and playing. It coped really well, so I’m delighted.”

That reprieve has allowed Graham, who has been beset by injuries in recent season, to set about reasserting himself in Scotland’s back three after losing his status as a guaranteed starter at the beginning of this year’s Six Nations.

“The competition in the Scotland team now is just through the roof, especially in the back-three positions, with Kyle Rowe, Jamie Dobie and Kyle Steyn playing unbelievable through at Glasgow, they’re carving it up every week,” said Graham.

“For myself, I need to keep pushing. It’s probably easy getting back to where I was but the hard part is staying at that level. I’ve just got to keep working away, keeping hammering away at training and showing what I can do.”

The Scots will wrap up their inaugural Nations Championship campaign against Argentina at Allianz Stadium in London next Sunday after finishing fourth in the northern hemisphere table with four wins and two defeats against the heavyweights of South Africa and New Zealand.

“That New Zealand game was obviously frustrating,” said Graham. “I don’t think we really showed what we were about.

“And then we never really got going again in the Australia game so it was just nice to go out and put a real attacking performance out there (against Japan), especially as a backline, to be able to go out and do what we’re good at.”

title: Héctor "Pochola" Silva into World Rugby Hall of Fame
article_text:
World Rugby announced that it will welcome seven players into its Hall of Fame over the coming months. One of them is from the Americas. It is former Puma and Pumas coach, Héctor “Pochola” Silva. Rugby was in his blood with his contribution to Argentine rugby also running deep at Los Tilos club.

Silva will be posthumously inducted in Buenos Aires on December 14 during the UAR annual dinner. He will become the seventh Argentine player inducted into the World Rugby Hall of Fame.

Pochola started playing rugby aged 14. At age 20, he earned his call-up to Los Pumas for the 1965 tour of South Africa. He was a Puma from 1965-1980 and earned 25 test caps.

On September 23, 2017, an emotional ceremony was held at the Los Tilos grounds, where the club’s main field, Pitch No. 1, was officially named “Héctor Pochola Silva.” Silva attended the tribute and expressed his gratitude for receiving such an honor during his lifetime. He passed away in May 2021 from COVID-19.

title: Afghanistan wins Bronze at Asian Rugby Sevens Cup 2026
article_text:
KABUL: Afghanistan’s national rugby team defeated Bangladesh 19-10 in its final match at the 2026 Asian Rugby Sevens Cup, securing third place in the tournament and the bronze medal.

The competition was held on Saturday and Sunday in Chinese Taipei (Taiwan), featuring four teams, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, the Philippines and Chinese Taipei.

In the final, the Philippines defeated host team Chinese Taipei 19-14 to claim the championship, finishing the tournament with five wins from five matches.

The final standings saw the Philippines take first place, Chinese Taipei finish second, Afghanistan secure third place and Bangladesh come fourth.

title: England star could miss Six Nations after latest injury setback
article_text:
Alex Mitchell is facing a lengthy spell on the sidelines after undergoing surgery on his latest hamstring injury, with the England scrum-half potentially set to miss the 2027 Six Nations.

The 29-year-old has been struggling with recurring hamstring problems throughout 2026 and is now facing an extended period of rehabilitation after going under the knife.

Mitchell picked up his latest injury while playing for Northampton Saints in their Gallagher PREM victory over Gloucester at Franklin’s Gardens on October 31.

He was forced off after just 21 minutes, with Jonny Weimann coming on as his replacement. The injury subsequently ruled him out of England’s Nations Championship squad for their November fixtures.

The Northampton scrum-half has since travelled to Finland to undergo surgery with Lasse Lempainen, a specialist in elite sporting injuries.

It is the fourth hamstring injury Mitchell has suffered this year.

He previously damaged the same hamstring against Ireland in February and Fiji in July, while also picking up an issue with his left hamstring during an England training camp in May.

Mitchell, who was Steve Borthwick's first-choice scrum-half last season, has managed to return ahead of schedule from previous injuries.

However, an estimated four-month rehabilitation would leave him with little time to force his way back into contention for the Six Nations.

England's campaign begins before Mitchell would be expected to return, although there is a possibility he could feature in the final two rounds against Wales and Scotland on March 6 and 13 respectively.

Borthwick now has three main options at scrum-half, with Jack van Poortvliet, Ben Spencer and Mitchell's Northampton teammate Archie McParland all available.

Van Poortvliet currently appears to be the leading candidate for the starting shirt, having been entrusted with the role during Mitchell's absence.

Tommy Freeman was a late withdrawal from England's victory over New Zealand yesterday after picking up a thigh niggle.

The winger was replaced in the starting XV by Cadan Murley around an hour before kick-off.

His availability for next week's Nations Championship finals weekend rematch against the All Blacks remains unclear.

title: Hollie Davidson named 'best referee' after decision left Argentina star fuming
article_text:
Hollie Davidson has been hailed as the "best referee in world rugby" after her impressive performance in France's clash with Argentina, which included a contentious decision that left Pumas captain Julian Montoya furious.

The Scottish official earned widespread praise for her handling of the contest in Paris, with former England captain Will Carling among those to single her out for special recognition.

One incident in particular caught the attention of viewers, with Davidson standing firm after Montoya angrily protested a decision at the breakdown.

With France leading 26-10, a penalty was awarded against the Argentina skipper following a chaotic passage of play at a ruck.

France winger Louis Bielle-Biarrey had initially flown into the breakdown, before Montoya then attempted to steal possession, only for Davidson to penalise him for going off his feet.

The Argentina captain was incensed by the decision, repeatedly shouting "It's the same!" as he pointed out what he believed was a similar infringement by Bielle-Biarrey moments earlier.

Davidson was unmoved, telling Montoya: "Off feet, you're driving over the breakdown."

The exchange came during a difficult spell for Argentina, with Montoya subsequently sent to the sin bin.

Former France hooker Benjamin Kayser, working as co-commentator, was full of praise for Davidson's handling of the situation.

"Hollie Davidson, having absolutely none of it!" he exclaimed.

"Julian Montoya was fuming at this decision. But I think she is absolutely spot on.

"The clearout from Louis Bielle-Biarrey, then [Montoya] goes around and he dives on it."

Davidson's performance throughout the contest attracted considerable attention on social media, with many supporters praising her authority, communication and consistency.

Former England captain Carling was particularly impressed, suggesting she had outperformed every other official involved in the weekend's international fixtures.

Writing on X, he said: "One other observation about all the great games yesterday - how good was Hollie Davidson - I thought she was easily the best referee - eagle eyed, calm, authoritative when needed, sympathetic when needed - and used the TMO quickly and precisely - loved it."

His assessment prompted a wave of agreement from rugby supporters, who were similarly impressed by the Scottish referee's display.

One fan responded: "She was absolutely tip top."

Another wrote: "Absolutely. She is getting the big games based on merit alone. That's all the game wants - the best refs. She is one them."

A third simply declared: "She's fantastic!"

Others suggested Davidson's rise through the refereeing ranks was an encouraging sign for rugby more generally.

"Apart from her own achievements, it reflects really well on the progress the game has made," one supporter wrote.

Another added: "She is a brilliant ref."

One fan praised her no-nonsense approach, writing: "Well said. She's a top ref, takes no nonsense."

Davidson, 34, has established herself as one of the most highly regarded officials in international rugby, earning increasingly prominent appointments in the men's game.

Her latest performance only strengthened that reputation, with another supporter writing: "100% agree - at only 34yo Hollie Davidson is a great example for those who wish to officiate at all levels in the game that we have grown to know and love."

title: Andy Farrell praises Sam Prendergast’s response after South Africa criticism
article_text:
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Andy Farrell believes Sam Prendergast emerged from a pre-match storm fuelled by South Africa’s coaching staff to show exactly what he is capable of.

Fly-half Prendergast ultimately landed the decisive penalty in Saturday’s statement 20-17 win over the world champions in Dublin after avoiding retrospective punishment for a hip-drop tackle against Fiji.

Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus branded Prendergast’s challenge “terrible” but predicted he would be cleared to play on a “technicality” during a controversial press conference on Monday.

Erasmus’ assistant Mzwandile Stick continued the criticism on Friday, saying: “If that was a Fijian player, he would be sitting in Fiji now doing some extra lessons of how to tackle.”

Ireland head coach Farrell made clear his unhappiness with the inflammatory comments from the opposition camp as he praised Prendergast’s response.

“I didn’t like all that,” he said. “It carried on during the week as well, didn’t it? I didn’t like all that about Sam because Sam was cleared, and I was there while he was cleared.

“Sam’s done nothing wrong and I was so proud of him in the sense that he played like that.

“Nothing bothered him, I thought he was excellent. He had the courage to play the balls out the back, play quickly, and play to space. I thought it was an excellent game from him all round.”

After Robert Baloucoune scored two first-half tries and Ronan Kelleher added another, Prendergast nervelessly split the posts from distance in the 54th minute before a heroic defensive display secured victory.

Prendergast, 23, also received a glowing endorsement from half-back partner Jamison Gibson-Park.

“He’s come on leaps and bounds I think in the last little while,” said the scrum-half.

“He’s just taken it all in his stride and the most impressive thing is he’s just able to bounce into the next moment and I know that’s something he’s working hard on but I’m pretty proud of the guy.

“He’s been through a lot and he’s playing some good footy so I’m very happy for him.”

Ireland laid down a marker ahead of next year’s World Cup with an overdue – and thoroughly deserved – success over one of rugby’s top-ranked nations.

Their scrum was comprehensively outmuscled by South Africa in a 24-13 Dublin defeat last November, while they have lost their last four meetings with New Zealand and last two with France.

Farrell has now won four of six encounters with the Springboks after celebrating another memorable victory of his reign, secured in front of a capacity Aviva Stadium crowd.

“It’s another massive game so it has to be up there (as one of the best),” he said.

“It’s what we also expect of ourselves – not to beat South Africa but to keep growing and delivering, certainly at home. It certainly matters a lot to us.”

Captain Dan Sheehan, who started at number eight for the first time at Test level, relished the challenge of taking on a different role having won his previous 42 caps at hooker.

He said: “It wasn’t perfect by any means but something different keeps your mind busy and almost gives me a distraction from thinking about the game too much.

“I was pretty happy with how the lads fronted up, especially in the pack. I thought we kept our calm pretty well at times and backed ourselves when it mattered.

“We talked about it all week, about making sure we front up on big days like this and the privilege of having the world champions in our back garden and for lads to show up meant a lot.”

Ireland will play Australia in the Nations Championship fifth-place final at Twickenham on Friday evening.

title: Wales star Tomos Williams stood down with immediate effect
article_text:
Steve Tandy has provided an injury update on Tomos Williams after the Wales scrum-half has emerged as a doubt for next weekend’s clash against Japan.

Williams suffered a groin problem during Wales’ dramatic 29-26 defeat against Australia at Principality Stadium.

Wales head coach Tandy confirmed that the Saracens player's injury will be assessed over the coming days.

His absence would be another concern after the Wallabies brought them back down to earth just seven days after ending their 73-year wait for a victory over the All Blacks.

Speaking after the match, a subdued Tandy offered a relatively positive initial assessment but also mentioned the possibility of replacing Williams for the encounter against Japan.

“Tomos is just a bit tight in his groin,” admitted Tandy.

“We will assess that as we go, but we have got options.

“I thought Reuben (Morgan-Williams) did really well when he came on.”

Wales now face a nervous wait over Williams’ availability as their attention is firmly fixed on the Brave Blossoms at Allianz Stadium.

Potentially, Tandy may have to reshuffle, which could see Reuben Morgan-Williams or uncapped Che Hope in line if the experienced scrum-half fails to recover.

Captain Dewi Lake scored twice, with Blair Murray and Ryan Elias also crossing, but those four crosses were not enough to prevent Wales from suffering a narrow three-point defeat.

Tandy confirmed that changes are likely for Wales’ final Nations Championship match as he looks to freshen up his side following a demanding campaign.

“We will definitely look at that,” continued Tandy.

“The boys have got a couple days off now.

“We will look at the changing room and see where we are with injuries.

“We will definitely freshen things up for next week.”

Tandy will select his Wales side to face Japan on Thursday.

title: Wales to make changes for Nations Championship finale as fringe stars to get chance
article_text:
Steve Tandy has vowed to rotate his side for their final Nations Championship match against Japan in London next week.

Wales will take on the Brave Blossoms for the fifth time in 16 months, as the two sides play for ninth place in Twickenham next week. Tandy had already teed up making changes in his press duties last week, before confirming he would rotate to face Eddie Jones' side.

Having beaten Japan before the historic win over New Zealand, Wales weren't quite able to get over the line in their third match against Australia - falling just short in a thrilling 29-26 defeat.

However, Tandy will be confident of a repeat victory against Japan - regardless of changes - after Eddie Jones' side conceded 145 points to England and Scotland in the last two weeks.

Naturally, the Wales coach reiterated that it was all about performance, first and foremost.

“We’ve got to build on this and be better than we were this week in terms of our performance," he said. "It’s something we can’t get away from.

“We’ve had a good tournament so far, and we’re disappointed with today. But we want to finish on a high, and that will only be as good as the performance we produce.

“I can rotate the team and we’ll still put in a performance. Ultimately, we’ve got to perform. It doesn’t matter who wears the shirt – we’ve got to perform.

“Whenever we put a team out, the objective is to win a Test match. That will be no different next Saturday.”

Scrum-half Tomos Williams could be one player who doesn't feature next week, having left the field with a groin injury early in the second half.

The Saracens star will be assessed, as Tandy considers changes for next Saturday's match.

“I thought the boys did pretty well," said Tandy. "We’re growing as a team and we’re a young group. Think about where we were 12 months ago.

“The boys have got a couple of days off now, so we’ll look at the changing room and see where we are with injuries.

“We’ll definitely freshen things up for next week.”

Tandy sang the praises of low-cap players like Reuben Morgan-Williams, Kane James and Louie Hennessey - who all came off the bench for solid minutes against Australia.

There could be an opportunity for similarly inexperienced players to get opportunities next week if Tandy does rotate heavily.

Cardiff prop Rhys Barratt, Scarlets wing Macs Page and Dragons duo Che Hope and Aneurin Owen are the uncapped options in the squad.

There are also a handful of players - such as Ellis Mee, Tom Rogers and the recalled Seb Davies - who have yet to feature this autumn.

title: All Blacks equal lowest-ever World Ranking; Northern trio close in on Boks
article_text:
Saturday’s record 37-12 defeat to England in the final round of the pool stages of the Nations Championship has sent New Zealand down to fifth in the World Rugby Men’s Rankings, equalling their lowest-ever position.

New Zealand were last ranked fifth at the end of August 2022, after Argentina inflicted a first-ever home loss on them in Christchurch, 25-18.

Rather than New Zealand, it’s the three strongest teams in the Six Nations who are now breathing down the necks of the Springboks.

Following their 20-17 win over the world champions in Dublin, Ireland have moved up to second on 89.98 points, a gain of two places and 1.28 points. They are 0.47 points ahead of France, who remain in third, but with an improved score of 89.51, after their 45-17 win over Argentina, while England are up one place to fourth, on 89.04 points.

With just 0.74 points separating the Springboks from France, their opponents in next Sunday’s Nations Championship final, the teams are not only playing for the inaugural title but also to finish the year as the world’s No.1 team. Ireland still have a say in that but will get precious few points, if any, for beating the lower-ranked Australia in Friday’s fifth place decider.

The rest of the top 10 is unchanged, but 11th place is now the domain of Japan, who are ranked higher than Italy, following the Azzurri’s home defeat to Fiji.

Meanwhile, Samoa’s forward momentum continues, with a thumping 90-22 Nations Cup win over Spain being rewarded with a two-place rise to 14th. Earlier in the tournament, they were ranked 19th.

The only other major change involves USA, who fall a couple of places to 16th as a result of their 38-10 defeat to fellow Nations Cup champions Georgia.

However, Tonga have swapped places with Spain after they overcame Hong Kong China 55-19, with the Ikale ‘Tahi now 18th and Spain 19th.

title: Springboks issue public denial to Erasmus claims as World Rugby urged to act
article_text:
The Springboks have denied there was any communication between the coaching box and Rassie Erasmus on Saturday - despite the head coach seemingly talking all the way through his watchalong from a Dublin hotel.

Erasmus had been handed a six-match ban in the build-up to the Test match between South Africa and Ireland due to comments he made in the aftermath of defeat to France last weekend. You can read more about that here.

Subsequently, the double World Cup winner was forced to watch events away from the Aviva Stadium, hosting a live watchalong with around 90,000 signed-up supporters. Erasmus spoke briefly before the game and at half-time, but muted the sound on the live stream for the vast majority of the game.

He also appeared to be conversation with someone, but South Africa coach Felix Jones has denied that was the case.

“No, no, I had the mics,” Irishman Jones said, who was reportedly unable to elaborate on the answer as media officers stepped in. “I think Ireland did really well to capitalise off a couple of our exits where we weren’t quite accurate.

“I think we might have given away one or two penalties trying to get out, and Ireland capitalised off it really well and were really accurate with what they did off the back of it, some clever stuff there. I thought they attacked well so full credit to Andrew Goodman, I thought he did a great job.“Then I would say the other area was probably the breakdown, and I felt that they just got a little bit more speed, a little bit quicker in. We were caught sealing a couple of times. I need to watch them back to see why that happened.

“Probably those are the two big ones, but having said that, you know, the Canan Moodie try/no try, he’s in touch... We’d a couple of opportunities right towards the end, with quite a bit of momentum. It was still within our control if we were able to convert, so really close game, but can’t complain.

“I thought Ireland won those key moments that I just mentioned there, and you can see they’re clearly... Andy has a really strong coaching team.

“The breakdown... I know Paul [O’Connell] is all over the breakdown. I know Andrew [Goodman] really well as well. So it’s two really great assistant coaches there, doing a good job.”

Erasmus was not allowed any matchday involvement under the terms of his World Rugby ban - which included coaching, direct or indirect contact with the team management or players, entering the stadium, coaches' box, playing enclosure or technical area.

While it is unclear who Erasmus was communicating with during the game, some fans have suggested World Rugby should investigate if he has breached the terms of his ban.

The coach wore earbuds throughout and leant in behind his laptop while communicating, with his mouth hidden from shot.

He was also seen on his phone several times throughout the game.

title: ATP Calendar 2027: Key Men’s Tennis Tournament Dates
article_text:
The 2027 men’s tennis calendar runs from the Australian Open through to the Nitto ATP Finals in Turin, with the year built around the four Grand Slams, nine Masters 1000s and the season-ending finale.

The order matters as much as the dates: hard courts open the year, clay takes over through spring, grass gets its turn in June and July, then the tour finishes with the North American hard-court swing and the indoor run in Asia and Europe.

The Australian Open is first up in Melbourne, with Opening Week from 10 to 16 January and the main draw starting on 17 January.

From there, the season moves quickly into the Sunshine Double, with Indian Wells and Miami setting the early hard-court rhythm before the tour switches to clay in Monte-Carlo, Madrid and Rome, then on to Roland-Garros.

Here, readers can find more in-depth information on the 2027 ATP season schedule, with comprehensive coverage of the major tournaments at William Hill throughout the year.

Australian Open 2027 is the season’s first Grand Slam tournament, staged in Melbourne from 10 to 31 January, with the main draw running from 17 to 31 January.

That opening stretch gives players the first big title of the year and, for the fans, the first proper marker for who has arrived ready to play from ball one.

Indian Wells runs from 3 to 14 March in Indian Wells, before Miami follows from 17 to 28 March in Miami Gardens. Together, they form the Sunshine Double, the hard-court double-header that asks players to stay sharp over two straight Masters 1000s.

The clay swing starts with the Rolex Monte-Carlo Masters from 4 to 11 April at Monte-Carlo Country Club, and the venue keeps the event’s setting as distinctive as ever.

Madrid follows from 21 April to 2 May, then Rome runs from 5 to 16 May. These three events are the spine of the clay season before the field heads to Paris.

Roland-Garros runs from 23 May to 6 June as the clay-court major in Paris. It completes the run from Monte-Carlo through Madrid and Rome into the French Open, the stretch of the season that shapes the leading clay-court contenders.

Wimbledon is the only grass-court event in the main table, and the 2027 Championships run from 28 June to 11 July.

That short grass window keeps the surface change sharp: there is not much room for adjustment, and the players who find the rhythm early usually make life easiest for themselves.

The custom schedule also includes Queen’s, which sits outside the 14-event main table but still matters in the grass-season build-up. The ATP 500 at Queen’s runs from 14 to 20 June, giving the leading names a key tune-up before Wimbledon gets going.

Toronto opens the North American hard-court swing from 1 to 12 August, with the men’s Canadian Open in Toronto in 2027. That makes Toronto the first major checkpoint before Cincinnati and New York.

Cincinnati follows from 12 to 22 August, and the US Open comes next from 29 August to 12 September in New York.

The season’s final stretch heads to Shanghai from 6 to 17 October.[1] Paris closes the indoor Masters run from 1 to 7 November, with the indoor Paris Masters staged in Nanterre in the Paris area. The Nitto ATP Finals bring the curtain down in Turin from 14 to 21 November.

The first half of 2027 belongs to the hard courts of Melbourne, Indian Wells and Miami before the clay swing takes over through Monte-Carlo, Madrid, Rome and Roland-Garros.

Wimbledon stands alone as the grass major, and the season then resets for the North American hard-court run through Toronto, Cincinnati and the US Open.

Shanghai, the indoor Paris Masters in Nanterre and Turin complete the closing run, which means the year ends the same way it began: with elite players having to stay healthy, stay sharp and keep the level high when the calendar barely leaves time to breathe.

title: WTA Calendar 2027: Key Women’s Tennis Tournament Dates
article_text:
The 2027 WTA calendar stretches across 55 events in 26 countries and territories, and every combined WTA 1000 event will award equal prize money for the first time.

The season runs all the way through the WTA Finals in Charlotte, North Carolina, so the finish line comes with a new host and a fresh backdrop at Spectrum Center.

That gives the year a clear spine: Melbourne starts the major swings, Doha and Dubai lead February, Indian Wells and Miami drive the spring hard-court run, Madrid and Rome set up Roland-Garros, Queen’s offers a short grass-court lead-in, and the North American summer rolls from Montréal to Cincinnati before New York takes over.

The Australian Open begins the Grand Slam season in Melbourne from 17 January to 31 January 2027 on hard courts. Brisbane follows first in the Australian swing, with Adelaide and Hobart also filling the early-season schedule before the tour moves into the Middle East.

The Qatar Open in Doha runs from 7 February to 13 February, then the Dubai Tennis Championships takes over from 14 February to 20 February.

The month belongs to that Doha-Dubai pairing, and the back-to-back WTA 1000 stops give the opening quarter of the season a strong rhythm before the tour heads into the American hard-court stretch, which is popular with sports betting punters.

The BNP Paribas Open at Indian Wells sits from 3 March to 14 March 2027 and remains an outdoor hard-court WTA 1000 at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden.

Miami follows from 16 March to 28 March, and the women’s event opens a day earlier than the men’s draw while the women’s singles final lands on 27 March.

That creates the usual Sunshine Double feel: Indian Wells first, Miami second, both on hard courts and both carrying the weight of the first major American swing of the year.

The clay-court stretch begins with the Mutua Madrid Open from 20 April to 2 May, then the Internazionali BNL d’Italia in Rome from 4 May to 16 May. Both are WTA 1000 events, and both are key staging points before the clay season reaches its peak in Paris.

Roland-Garros runs from 23 May to 6 June 2027, with the women’s singles final on 5 June. That puts the French Open right at the centre of the spring clay swing, and it remains the biggest test before the grass-court switch.

A WTA 500 at Queen’s from 7 June to 13 June provides the short lead-in to the grass season before Wimbledon. Wimbledon is scheduled for 28 June to 11 July 2027 in London on grass.

The grass block is shorter than the clay swing, but it still demands a fast adjustment in timing and surface instincts. Wimbledon brings the season’s sharpest change of pace, and it arrives after just enough grass-court preparation to make the transition feel meaningful rather than rushed.

The Canadian Open women’s draw is in Montréal from 1 August to 12 August 2027, with the tournament played at IGA Stadium and an 11,500-seat setting adding to the scale of the event.

Cincinnati follows from 12 August to 22 August, keeping the WTA 1000 action rolling straight after Montréal.

The US Open then starts on 29 August and runs through 12 September in New York on outdoor hard courts. That end-to-end summer stretch gives the hard-court season a long runway, with Montréal and Cincinnati feeding directly into the final Grand Slam of the year.

The autumn swing opens in Beijing with the China Open from 29 September to 10 October at the China National Tennis Center. Wuhan follows from 11 October to 17 October, turning the close of the regular season into a back-to-back WTA 1000 double-header.

Charlotte then hosts the WTA Finals for the first time, with the event set for 2027 through 2029 at Spectrum Center and additional programming at Charlotte Convention Center.

The WTA Finals run from 10 November to 14 November, giving the season its last big stage in North Carolina.

The 2027 schedule is built around a few key anchors rather than a long list of disconnected stops.

Australia starts the year, Doha and Dubai head February, the Sunshine Double shapes March, the clay run climbs through Madrid and Rome into Paris, Queen’s leads into Wimbledon, and the hard-court summer finishes with Montréal, Cincinnati and New York.

The most notable structural change is the equal-prize-money milestone across every combined WTA 1000 event.

That matters because it gives the tour’s biggest non-Slam stops the same financial footing on both sides of the draw, which should keep the top events feeling properly loaded all year.

title: Renowned News Outlet Strikes $11 Million ATP Deal To Promote Tennis Across Its Home Nation
article_text:
French tennis enthusiasts are set to be treated to a familiar name on their television screens. beIN Sports has won back the rights to the ATP Tour in France from 2028, and it hasn’t cost them an arm and a leg. According to L’Equipe, the Franco-Qatari channel will pay a little under 10 million euros, roughly 11 million dollars, a year across a four-year deal running to 2031, a deliberately restrained outlay for such a prized property.

The move, confirmed on 9 November, amounts to a homecoming of sorts. beIN Sports will broadcast the ATP in France before Eurosport got the rights, which means that the rights to the men’s tour are back on the channel. This time, however, it is coming back on its own terms – at a price that is more indicative of a leaner, more disciplined era in the business of broadcast rights than any of the crazy bidding that has occurred in the past few years.

The sum says a good deal about beIN’s current thinking. It sits only marginally above the roughly 5 million euros a year that the outgoing rights holder, Eurosport, has been paying, and it barely registers against the budgets the channel has shed elsewhere. A few years ago, beIN walked away from a contract in Ligue 1 that was worth about 85.6 million dollars a year and has recently lost a contract in La Liga that was worth some 34.9 million dollars, giving it much more freedom to pick and choose its fights.

But it’s a mantra that’s become familiar to Yousef al-Obaidly, head of beIN Sports France, who has always said that one should spend smartly, not buy rights for the sake of buying rights. Securing the men’s tour for a modest fee, having stepped back from costlier football deals, fits neatly into that philosophy. For beIN, it is a way of strengthening its sporting line-up without the financial exposure that top-tier football now demands, a trade-off the channel appears increasingly comfortable making.

All nine ATP Masters 1000 events will be broadcast on beIN from 2028, and all ATP 500 and the Next Gen ATP Finals will also be broadcast on beIN, which is also being reported as having the ATP Finals as part of the deal at the end of the season. It’s a complete men’s offering, a package that will transform the sport’s presence at the start of the decade in France and round off a tennis collection that the broadcaster has been steadily assembling over the past few years.

beIN Sports is no newcomer to the game. The broadcaster already has the rights to the WTA Tour and to Wimbledon, so this adds the men’s circuit to the mix for a nearly full calendar. It will be a great selling point for subscribers as the majority of the top events of the season will come together under one roof starting in 2028, minus a few exceptions, when sports coverage is spread out across increasingly more platforms.

For Eurosport, the deal brings a long association with the ATP towards its end. Next year, the Warner Bros. Discovery-owned channel will air one final season of the men’s tour, but not everything is moving over at the same time.

Two French ATP 250 tournaments have been confirmed for Tennis Channel, and Eurosport has secured the future of the Australian Open and the US Open beyond 2030, ensuring it will have a role to play in the sport even after it stops hosting ATP events.

The upshot is that French coverage will be split across more than one home from 2028, with two of the four Grand Slams staying where they are while the week-to-week tour action moves on, a division viewers will have to get used to.

The reshuffle reflects a wider trend in the sports-rights market, where broadcasters have become more hesitant to pay top dollar, and sellers are forced to agree to lower figures than the glory days dictated.

While the headline fee isn’t jaw-dropping, but the committed signing until 2031 is a solid piece of stability for the ATP. The bottom line for French TV viewers is even more straightforward, as the way to watch the men’s game will go through beIN Sports from 2028.

There will surely be subscription fee and reach questions, as beIN is behind a paywall, but at least it ends the uncertainty that hung over the tour’s French future.

title: Thailand’s ‘View’ Kunlavut reclaims world No 1 badminton ranking
article_text:
Thailand’s badminton star Kunlavut “View” Vitidsarn has reclaimed the world No 1 spot in the men’s singles rankings following the latest update announced by the Badminton World Federation (BWF) on Tuesday (November 24).

The 25-year-old Thai shuttler moved up from second place with 91,585 ranking points, overtaking France’s Christo Popov, who dropped to second with 89,932 points.

Kunlavut’s return to the summit follows a series of impressive performances throughout 2026, highlighted by his historic Asian Games gold medal and runner-up finish at the Hong Kong Open.

Kunlavut reached the final of the Hong Kong Open 2026 but was forced to withdraw from the championship match against Denmark’s Anders Antonsen on Sunday (November 22) because of a back injury.

Antonsen was consequently awarded the title by walkover, while Kunlavut finished runner-up at the BWF World Tour Super 500 tournament.

Despite the injury setback, the Thai star earned enough ranking points to regain the world No 1 position, marking his fourth spell at the top of the men’s singles rankings.

Kunlavut first became world No 1 on June 3, 2025, following his Singapore Open triumph, becoming the first Thai men’s singles badminton player to reach the top of the world rankings.

He returned to No 1 in March 2026 following his run to the All England Open semi-finals before reclaiming the position again after winning gold at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.

On September 29, Kunlavut defeated Singapore’s Loh Kean Yew 21-12, 21-16 to secure Thailand’s first-ever Asian Games gold medal in men’s singles badminton.

His latest rise to the top caps another remarkable chapter in his career and underlines his standing among the world’s elite badminton players.

title: Malaysia's World Tour Finals contingent shrinks to just two pairs
article_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia will have just two pairs at next month's World Tour Finals in Hangzhou, China, marking the country's smallest representation since 2023 despite another productive season on the international badminton circuit.

Men's doubles Goh Sze Fei-Nur Izzuddin Rumsani and women's doubles Pearly Tan-M. Thinaah are the only Malaysians to have secured qualifying spots for the Dec 9-13 showpiece, following the conclusion of the Hong Kong Open on Sunday.

After having six entries in 2024 and five last year, Malaysia's tally matches the joint-lowest representation since the BWF World Tour replaced the Super Series circuit in 2018, with just two pairs fielded in 2018, 2019 and 2023.

Although having more representatives does not necessarily guarantee success, the decline means fewer Malaysians will have the opportunity to compete against the season's best performers while reaping substantial financial and ranking rewards.

This year's World Tour Finals will offer a record US$3.5mil (RM14.41 million) in total prize money, an increase of US$500,000 (RM2.06 million) from last year, making it the richest tournament in badminton history.

The doubles champions stand to pocket a staggering US$294,000 (RM1.21 million) per pair, almost three times the US$107,3000 (RM442,000) awarded to the winners of this year's prestigious All England, a Super 1000 tournament.

Even finishing fourth and last in the group stage is worth approximately US$24,500 (RM100,900) for a doubles pair, considerably more than the US$19,000 (RM78,200) earned by the runners-up at last Sunday's Hong Kong Open.

The ranking benefits are equally attractive, with a fourth-place group finish earning 7,800 points, equivalent to reaching the final of a Super 500 tournament and slightly more than making the semi-finals of a Super 750 event.

For those who advance further, the financial rewards increase significantly, with the doubles runners-up earning approximately US$140,000 (RM576,500) and losing semi-finalists US$70,000 (RM288,300) per pair.

While Malaysia's representation may be limited this year, both qualifying pairs have strong credentials to challenge for honours.

World No. 5 Sze Fei-Izzuddin will be making their second appearance, having finished runners-up on their debut in 2024.

The independent pair came agonisingly close to becoming Malaysia's first World Tour Finals champions that year before losing to Denmark's Kim Astrup-Anders Skaarup Rasmussen in the final.

They failed to qualify last year but have bounced back strongly this season, winning the Indonesia Masters in January and the prestigious Indonesia Open in June.

Their consistency was further underlined by runners-up finishes at the Malaysia Masters and French Open, helping them secure a return to Hangzhou.

Pearly-Thinaah, meanwhile, will be making their fifth appearance at the season-ending tournament, although their breakthrough only came last year when they reached the semi-finals for the first time.

The world No. 4 previously failed to progress beyond the group stage in 2021, 2022 and 2024, while missing qualification in 2023.

Their campaign last year ended with a semi-final defeat to Japan's Yuki Fukushima-Mayu Matsumoto.

However, Pearly-Thinaah will head into this year's edition in encouraging form after capturing three titles, including Sunday's Hong Kong Open triumph.

They also won the Indonesia Masters and Denmark Open, besides finishing runners-up at the French Open and Taiwan Open.

Malaysia have yet to produce a World Tour Finals champion since the competition entered the World Tour era in 2018.

The country's closest attempts came in 2024, when Sze Fei-Izzuddin and mixed doubles pair Chen Tang Jie-Toh Ee Wei both reached the finals but settled for runners-up finishes.

Last year, Pearly-Thinaah and Tang Jie-Ee Wei made the semi-finals but were unable to progress further.

title: Aaron Tai-Roy King eye top 10 after stunning World Tour start
article_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: New men's doubles sensation Aaron Tai-Yap Roy King, buoyed by their impressive World Tour start, is looking to break into the top 10, aided by a favourable 15-point scoring system set to be introduced next year.

Aaron Tai-Roy King, who began their partnership at the European swing last month, won their first tournaments as a pair at the Arctic Open before adding the Kumamoto Masters title two weeks ago. Both were Super 500 events.

The Malacca-born duo have made a meteoric rise in the world rankings and are now ranked world No. 34 after playing in just six World Tour events.

After finishing their season at the Hong Kong Open last week, where they reached the last 16, Aaron Tai-Roy King will hope to continue their climb in the rankings and chase more honours under the 15-point scoring system, which favours their fast, aggressive style of play.

"We hope to push for the top 10 next year. We have a little advantage but in the 15-point scoring, anything can happen, so we need to be more focused," said the soft-spoken Aaron Tai at the Academy Badminton Malaysia (ABM) on Tuesday.

Aaron Tai also expressed surprise at their progress and attributed their success on the World Tour to their fluid combination and speed.

"I am definitely surprised by the way we have progressed because we have just started as a pair," added Aaron Tai.

"This was possible because his gameplay and mine are almost similar. We are fast and can combine well (on court)."

However, the 20-year-old former world junior champion also wants to iron out some of his weaknesses, especially his unforced errors and tendency to become too desperate to attack.

"I need to improve my consistency and also reduce errors. I also need to be patient when executing my shots and not rush," said Aaron Tai.

National men's doubles head coach Herry Iman Pierngadi was impressed with their speedy progress and made them permanent members of the squad after they reached the semi-finals of their third tournament, the Super 500 Hylo Open in Saarbrucken, Germany, last month.

Herry also believes their aggressive nature will make them Malaysia's most dangerous pair and even rated the youngsters higher than their seniors — world No. 4 Aaron Chia-Soh Wooi Yik and world No. 7 Man Wei Chong-Tee Kai Wun.

Their current world No. 34 ranking should still earn them a place in the Malaysia Open, scheduled for Jan 21-31, despite the tournament's top 32 cut-off for men's doubles pairs.

This is because both players are also ranked inside the top 32 with other partners. Aaron Tai is ranked No. 23 with Kang Khai Xing, while Roy King is No. 28 with Wan Arif Junaidi.

However, these two combinations will not be entered for the Super 1000 event, allowing Aaron Tai-Roy King to secure a place in the tournament.

title: Indonesia Sends Three Entries to $3.5 Million BWF World Tour Finals
article_text:
Indonesia Sends Three Entries to $3.5 Million BWF World Tour Finals

Jakarta. Indonesia is set to field five badminton players across three categories at the prestigious BWF World Tour Finals in Hangzhou, China, from Dec. 9 to 13, following the conclusion of the Race to Finals qualification standings at the 2026 Hong Kong Open.

Indonesia's representatives are Alwi Farhan in men's singles, Fajar Alfian and Muhammad Shohibul Fikri in men's doubles, and Amallia Cahaya Pratiwi and Siti Fadia Silva Ramadhanti in women's doubles.

The five shuttlers will be looking to end Indonesia's three-edition absence from the tournament's championship matches. The country's last finalists were Anthony Sinisuka Ginting in men's singles and Mohammad Ahsan and Hendra Setiawan in men's doubles, who finished as runners-up in 2022.

Alwi has emerged as one of Indonesia's standout performers this season, securing a place at the World Tour Finals for the first time in his career.

The 21-year-old faces formidable competition in men's singles, with a field featuring 2026 world champion Alex Lanier, defending champion Christo Popov and other leading players, including Kunlavut Vitidsarn and Anders Antonsen.

The men's singles lineup is particularly notable for the absence of Chinese representatives among the eight qualifiers. Europe, meanwhile, accounts for three places through French players Lanier and Popov and Denmark's Antonsen.

Fajar and Fikri will be looking to improve on their performance at the 2025 World Tour Finals, where they were eliminated in the group stage.

The Indonesian pair will compete against some of the world's leading men's doubles partnerships, including South Korea's Kim Won-ho and Seo Seung-jae, China's Liang Wei Keng and Wang Chang, and Malaysia's Goh Sze Fei and Nur Izzuddin Rumsani.

In women's doubles, Amallia and Siti Fadia secured their qualification after reaching the semifinals of the Hong Kong Open.

The Indonesian duo will face a competitive field that includes China's Liu Sheng Shu and Tan Ning, South Korea's Baek Ha-na and Lee So-hee, and Malaysia's Pearly Tan and Thinaah Muralitharan.

The 2026 BWF World Tour Finals offers a total prize pool of $3.5 million, up from $3 million in the previous edition.

The season-ending tournament brings together eight players or pairs in each of five categories. Participants are divided into two groups of four, with the top two finishers in each group advancing to the semifinals.

The final lineup remains subject to the Badminton World Federation's formal invitation and acceptance process.

Invitations are scheduled to be issued on Nov. 24, with players required to confirm their participation by Nov. 27. The group-stage draw is scheduled for Dec. 5.

title: Syed Modi International 2026: Full schedule, Indians in action, prize money, and all you need to know
