title: Lakshya Sen On Podium For Third Time With Hong Kong Open 2026 Bronze
article_text:
Lakshya Sen won bronze at the Hong Kong Open 2026 after losing the semifinal to Denmark’s Anders Antonsen, who became men’s singles champion.

Indian ace Lakshya Sen finished on the podium for the third time in the last month. Lakshya ended his Hong Kong Open 2026 campaign with a bronze medal in the men’s singles. Sen’s third-place finish came after losing to Denmark’s Anders Antonsen in the Super 500 semifinals. Anders went on to win the Hong Kong championship after Thailand’s second seed, Kunlavut Vitidsarn, withdrew due to injury concerns. Lakshya, ranked World No. 11 in the latest BWF World Rankings, has already secured his place at the BWF World Tour Finals before the semifinals. The Finals will be held in Hangzhou, China, from 9 to 13 December.

The World No.3 Danish player has also qualified for the World Tour Finals. He is ranked 4th for the Hangzhou Finals. He defeated Sen with 21-13 and 21-13 in both sets, winning the men’s singles semifinals. Sen’s campaign ended with a bronze medal in the Hong Kong Open. The final did not happen at the Super 500 as Kunlavut pulled out due to injury, and Antonsen was declared the winner.

Sen moved to sixth place in the Race to Finals standings after winning back-to-back BWF titles. The 25-year-old won the Hylo Open 2026 men’s singles title in Germany, and two weeks later he won the Kumamoto Masters 2026 in Japan.

In the women’s singles, two-time Asian Champion, China’s Wang Zhiyi defended her title and defeated Thailand’s Pornpawee Chochuwong. Chochuwong beat India’s Rakshitha Ramraj in the quarterfinals. The 19-year-old won against World No.4 in her previous match, making it a memorable outing for her.

Indian shuttlers now turn to the Syed Modi India International in Lucknow from 24 to 29 November.

title: Lakshya Sen and PV Sindhu Qualify for BWF World Tour Finals 2026, India Set for Two-Pronged Challenge in Hangzhou
article_text:
India will have two representatives at the 2026 BWF World Tour Finals, with Lakshya Sen and PV Sindhu securing qualification for the prestigious season-ending tournament scheduled to take place in Hangzhou, China, from December 9 to 13.

Sen will compete in men’s singles, while Sindhu has booked her place in women’s singles. Their qualification marks an important moment for Indian badminton, with both players returning to the year-end championship for the first time since 2021.

The two berths also reflect contrasting but equally encouraging stories. Sen secured his place through a strong finish to the season, winning consecutive Super 500 titles in Germany and Japan. Sindhu, meanwhile, has rebuilt her form following an injury-disrupted period, returning to the world’s top six and producing some of her most consistent badminton in recent seasons.

With eight players competing in each singles discipline, the World Tour Finals bring together the season’s most successful performers for one final test.

For Lakshya Sen, qualification represents a significant turnaround after an inconsistent middle phase of the season.

The Indian began 2026 with an impressive run at the All England Open, reaching the final after defeating established opponents, including Shi Yuqi and Victor Lai. He eventually finished runner-up to Taiwan’s Lin Chun-yi.

However, a series of early exits at major tournaments and a shoulder injury disrupted his campaign. His withdrawal from the French Open in October further complicated his qualification prospects.

Sen responded with an outstanding finish, winning the Hylo Open in Germany before claiming the Kumamoto Masters Japan title. At the Hylo Open, he defeated Indonesia’s Jonatan Christie 21–17, 21–10 in the final, becoming the first Indian to win the tournament twice. In Japan, he continued his momentum by defeating Koki Watanabe in the title match.

The back-to-back titles transformed his position in the HSBC Race to Finals standings.

Sen entered the Hong Kong Open as the sixth-ranked player in the Race to Finals, holding 74,180 points. His qualification was subsequently confirmed after compatriot Kidambi Srikanth defeated Japan’s Koki Watanabe, one of the players challenging for the final qualification positions.

Sen continued his Hong Kong campaign, reaching the semifinals before losing to Denmark’s Anders Antonsen.

The 25-year-old will now return to the World Tour Finals after making his debut in 2021, when he reached the semifinals. His recent performances suggest that he will arrive in Hangzhou with considerable confidence.

The men's singles field is particularly competitive, featuring defending champion Christo Popov, Indonesia’s Alwi Farhan, Canada’s Victor Lai, Antonsen, Chou Tien-chen and Thailand’s Kunlavut Vitidsarn. Reigning World Champion Alex Lanier also qualifies through the automatic exemption.

Sindhu’s qualification is another major positive for Indian badminton.

The two-time Olympic medallist has worked her way back into the elite group after an injury-affected period that interrupted her progress. Her 2026 season has been built around consistency, with 10 quarterfinal appearances, two titles and a return to World No. 6.

Her most significant victories came at the Japan Open Super 750 and Hylo Open Super 500. At the Japan Open, Sindhu defeated Japan’s Akane Yamaguchi 21–17, 21–17 in the final to claim an important title.

She also demonstrated her ability to challenge the very best by taking world No. 1 An Se-young to three games in the French Open final, eventually losing 21–16, 11–21, 12–21.

Sindhu’s return to the World Tour Finals carries additional significance. She remains the only Indian player to have won the women’s singles title, having lifted the trophy in 2018 in Guangzhou.

Ranked fifth in the Race to Finals, she will enter the Hangzhou competition with the experience of having competed against the world's leading players for more than a decade.

The women's singles field will be led by South Korea’s An Se-young, who has enjoyed a remarkable 2026 season. The defending champion and reigning World Champion has dominated the circuit, making her the leading contender for another title.

China’s Wang Zhiyi and Chen Yufei, Japan’s Akane Yamaguchi and Tomoka Miyazaki, and Thailand’s Ratchanok Intanon and Pornpawee Chochuwong will add further depth to the competition.

While India’s singles representation is encouraging, the country will have no entries in the three doubles disciplines.

The biggest disappointment is the absence of Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty. The former world No. 1 pair won two Super 750 titles during 2026, at the Singapore Open and China Masters, but finished outside the qualification positions after competing in a reduced tournament schedule.

Their workload management and commitments to national team events affected their Race to Finals ranking.

India’s women’s doubles pair Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand, despite winning a bronze medal at the 2026 World Championships, also missed qualification.

The 2026 World Tour Finals will feature eight qualifiers in each discipline, divided into two groups of four. The group stage will be followed by semifinals and finals, with the championship concluding on December 13.

The tournament carries total prize money of USD 3.5 million, underlining its status as one of the most prestigious events on the badminton calendar.

For India, the challenge will rest on Sen’s late-season momentum and Sindhu’s experience at the highest level. Both have already demonstrated that they can compete with the world’s best.

The next step is to convert that form into a strong finish in Hangzhou. With two singles players back among the season’s elite, Indian badminton will have another opportunity to end 2026 on a high.

title: Gauff, Townsend Clinch USA BJK Cup Victory over Hungary
article_text:
Coco Gauff created a happy homecoming weekend in Delray Beach.

Delray Beach native Coco Gauff and Taylor Townsend clinched Billie Jean King Cup Qualifying victory for the U.S. on Sunday, defeating Hungarian doubles pair Anna Bondar and Dalma Galfi 6-4, 6-3 at the Delray Beach Tennis Center.

Ashlyn Krueger, ranked No. 41 in the world, capped the tie with a 6-2, 6-1, dead singles win over Adrienn Nagy, giving captain Lindsay Davenport a clean sweep in the tie.

“I think there was always this scenario that we would probably be up 2-0. Once that was the scenario, I was, like, of course, I’m going to play and try to just finish it 3-0,” Gauff said. “Yeah, I think we were both prepared to play with each other. We didn’t know what the end of Day 1 results would

have looked like. Maybe if it was 1-All, maybe I would have not played, because I would have had to play singles

30 minutes later. But, you know, it’s always that risk.

“I feel like Taylor and Lindsay were confident in my ability to play in doubles and potentially have to play singles after, but I’m really happy that they trusted me to step in and make the change. But, yeah, I’m really happy that I got to play with Taylor today.”

The U.S. joins seven nations advancing out of the Playoffs to the 2027 Qualifiers. The Qualifiers will be played in April, with the specific dates and ties to be announced.

title: Badminton: Pearly-Thinaah savour booster ahead of tough test at World Tour Finals
article_text:
PETALING JAYA: National women’s doubles aces Pearly Tan-M. Thinaah could not have picked a better time to rediscover their form and rhythm.

The world No. 4 pair reclaimed the Hong Kong Open crown yesterday, defeating Japan’s Sumire Nakade-Miyu Takahashi 22-20, 21-16 in 40 minutes at the Kai Tak Arena.

Winning the crown without dropping a game puts them in good stead ahead of next month’s season-ending World Tour Finals.

“It’s definitely a confidence boost for the World Tour Finals,” said Thinaah.

It was sweet revenge for the 2024 champions, who lost to the Japanese pair in the Taipei Open final in August.

The victory brought them their third title of the year and second in five weeks, following triumphs at the Indonesia Masters in January and Denmark Open last month.

Their unbeaten run in Hong Kong marked a welcome turnaround after a disappointing first-round exit at last week’s Japan Masters.

“This week, we really wanted to put last week behind us, come in fresh and be more focused.”

A heart-to-heart talk helped them regroup, with Pearly taking satisfaction in how they handled difficult situations and managed their emotions throughout the week.

That composure showed in the final when they saved a game point at 19-20 despite Pearly breaking her racquet.

They then pulled away from 14-14 in the second game to seal the title.

“There were still ups and downs in the first few matches, but the way we managed them was really positive,” said Thinaah.

“There was also a lot of communication between us, which really helped throughout the week.”

A sterner examination awaits at the Finals in Hangzhou from Dec 9-13, with China’s Liu Shengshu-Tan Ning, world champions Baek Ha-na-Lee So-hee of South Korea and Japan’s Yuki Fukushima-Mayu Matsumoto among the qualified contenders.

Fukushima-Matsumoto ended the Malaysians’ breakthrough semi-final run last year.

Pearly-Thinaah had previously exited at the group stage in 2021, 2022 and 2024, while missing qualification in 2023.

“We want to go back and focus on the next two weeks. There are still many things we need to work on.”

“These will be two crucial weeks for both of us – learning, supporting each other and handling our emotions. We’re really excited for the World Tour Finals,” added Thinaah.

title: ATP Finals: Carlos Alcaraz beats world number one Alexander Zverev to claim title
article_text:
Carlos Alcaraz outplayed world number one Alexander Zverev to end his wait for a first ATP Finals title and complete a remarkable post-injury return to the sport.

A season which began with Alcaraz becoming the youngest man to complete the career Grand Slam, before he was ruled out for more than four months with a wrist issue, ended with the Spaniard holding aloft another of the sport's biggest trophies.

Alcaraz, still wearing heavy strapping around his upper-left leg following his injury scare earlier in the week, collapsed to the ground in celebration after sealing a 6-2 7-6 (9-7) win in a dramatic second-set tie-break.

It was a statement victory over Zverev, who took advantage of Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner's injury absences to rise to the top of the rankings and claim his first two major titles.

It was a 14th successive win and a third-straight title triumph for seven-time major winner Alcaraz, who demonstrated beyond any doubt that he is back to his devastating best.

"Lifting this trophy is something I have been chasing for a really long time, it means the world to me," the 23-year-old said.

"I have been through really difficult moments with myself, with my team. For me it's been an amazing week.

"I couldn't finish the week in a better way."

It is just 84 days since Alcaraz made his return at the US Open in August after a lengthy spell on the sidelines.

Since that tournament, the current world number three has won 21 of his 22 matches and swept titles at four of the five tournaments he has entered.

With his latest victory, Alcaraz has become the youngest man to win all four Grand Slams and the season-ending Finals - and only the fourth in history.

Zverev, who ends 2026 with an ATP Tour-leading 69 match victories, had not dropped serve in four straight-set matches to reach the final.

But for much of the two-hour title decider, his greatest weapon was dismantled by a brilliant Alcaraz.

Alcaraz handled the occasion far better as he emerged from a tense start with a 4-1 double-break lead on his way to the first set.

The contrasting emotions of the two players were evident when Alcaraz wore a big grin after pulling off a between-the-legs lob that Zverev smashed into the net. At the other end of the court, the German threw away his racquet in disgust.

While Alcaraz danced to music during a change of ends, Zverev's frustrations only grew as, after winning back one of the two breaks of serve, he received a second time violation on his way to losing serve for a third successive game.

The top seed left the court after unravelling in the first set, having produced just three winners to 19 unforced errors in an inconsistent start.

Alcaraz's march to the title appeared inevitable as he took control of the second set with a fourth break of serve, but Zverev restored parity in the eighth game and kept his hopes alive by forcing a tie-break.

Overturning a 3-0 deficit in the tie-break, Zverev then won six straight points to arrive at three set points.

However, he failed to take all of them, including one on his own serve, before Alcaraz drove in a backhand winner on his second match point.

After picking himself off the floor, the Spaniard celebrated with his team in the stands after finally landing the title he had been chasing for four years.

In the doubles, French debutants Theo Arribage and Albano Olivetti lifted the trophy after a comeback victory against Marcelo Arevalo and Mate Pavic.

The sixth seeds recovered from losing the first set to win 3-6 7-6 (7-2) 10-6, ending the year with the most wins (59) and titles (seven) in men's doubles.

title: Carlos Alcaraz and Alexander Zverev’s ATP Finals prize money & ranking points revealed
article_text:
Carlos Alcaraz is the 2026 ATP Finals champion, defeating Alexander Zverev in Sunday’s final to triumph in Turin.

The final pitted two reigning Grand Slam champions against each other, with French Open and US Open champion Zverev, the world No 1, up against world No 3 and Australian Open winner Alcaraz.

Alcaraz was gunning for the first ATP Finals title of his career, having lost in the 2025 final, while Zverev was looking to win the title for the third time after previous triumphs in 2018 and 2021.

And, it was the Spaniard who triumphed inside the Inalpi Arena on Sunday, battling past a resilient Zverev claim a 6-2, 7-6(7) victory in the championship match.

With the tournament now over, we look at the ranking points and prize money that both men will take home from the tournament.

Want more from Tennis365? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for tennis coverage you can trust.

What ranking points did Zverev and Alcaraz win in Turin?

Significant ranking points were on off in Turin this year, with 200 points per round-robin victory and 1,500 points guaranteed for any unbeaten champion at the ATP Finals.

With both Alcaraz and Zverev unbeaten on their way to the final, 1,500 points was therefore guaranteed for the champion.

It was Alcaraz who claimed that full 1,500 points thanks to his victory, which includes a full 500 points alone for winning Sunday’s final against the German.

That means he finishes the year as the world No 3 on 7,600 points, just 350 points behind leading rival and world No 2 Jannik Sinner in the ATP Rankings.

Meanwhile, runner-up Zverev takes home 1,000 ranking points for finishing as the runner-up. He ends the season on 10,350 points in the ATP Rankings, comfortably sealing the year-end No 1 position for the first time in his career.

What prize money did Zverev and Alcaraz win in Turin?

With neither of the two losing a match up until the final, both had already banked significant prize money winnings ahead of Sunday’s showpiece match.

Both men received a participant fee of $338,000 for their event qualification, $405,000 per round-robin win, and $1,206,000 for their respective victories in Saturday’s semi-finals.

Meanwhile, for his runner-up finish, Zverev claims a not-insignificant $2,759,000 after an impressive showing at the final ATP Tour event of 2026.

title: Jannik Sinner OUT of the Australian Open? Alarming report suggests an extended lay-off
article_text:
Jannik Sinner was forced to abort the second half of the 2026 season due to a knee injury and the latest reports suggest he may also be out of action of a large part of next year.

Sinner has not struck a ball in anger since winning the Wimbledon final against Alexander Zverev in July, with the Italian ruled out with a knee problem that has proved to be more serious than initially feared.

His absence allowed Zverev to take over as world No 1, with his hopes of getting back on court now in doubt again after a report in Italian publication Gazzetta dello Sport suggesting the problems are far from over for Sinner.

The report suggests Sinner has been consulting with Finnish surgeon Lasse Lempainen and he may now be forced to undergo surgery to resolve the problem.

“There are various procedures that could be applied to Sinner,” reports Federica Cocchi.

“These range from entering the knee to check the condition of the external meniscus and possibly cleaning it, to what’s called a “Z-plasty,” which involves a small incision, as if a very tight rope were cut to release the tension.

“This procedure may also involve removing the underlying bursa, which may have accumulated fluid.

“The third option is certainly the riskiest: operating on the knee bone if it’s believed to be impinging on the bone.

“While this could be a curative measure, the downside is that the bone, in reaction, could form an even larger callus, further worsening the inflammation of the band. In short, if surgery is necessary, it’s best to make the decision quickly to avoid wasting any more precious time.

“Obviously, if Lempainen is required, returning to Australia would not be possible, but depending on the type of surgery, recovery and return to action times could vary, at least three months.”

The initial vibes coming from the Sinner camp was that his absence from the game would be brief when he confirmed he would miss the Canadian Masters in August, but the knee problem has ended up being significant.

There are strong suggestions in the report that Sinner may now try and target a return in the European clay court season in April, with his extended absence a huge blow if it is confirmed.

It would also mean he misses out on a huge pay-day, as he is guaranteed $1.5million just for appearing at the Six Kings Slam exhibition event in Saudi Arabia next month.

Sinner has yet to make any public comment on his, but he did suggest in a recent video on his YouTube channel that he was ‘a long way’ from getting back on court.

Realistically, Sinner would need to be back on court and practicing in late December to have a realistic chance of being fit for the Australian Open in mid-January, but that comeback date may look ambitious given the latest update from the respected course in Italy.

title: Nitto ATP Finals 2026 Prize Money Breakdown- How Much Will Carlos Alcaraz & Alexander Zverev Earn?
article_text:
Winning the ATP Finals trophy could earn one player $5.17 million, but even falling short of the championship does not mean walking away with a small payday. At the 2026 edition in Turin, a player who wins all three group-stage matches and reaches the semifinals is guaranteed $1.553 million, even if their title hopes end there.

With every victory carrying a separate financial reward, the season-ending tournament offers one of the most lucrative opportunities in men's tennis.

The 2026 Nitto ATP Finals, held from November 15 to 22 at the Inalpi Arena in Turin, Italy, features a record $15.75 million prize pool across singles and doubles.

The undefeated singles champion can collect $5,171,000, while the winning doubles team can split $959,300. But what makes this year's prize money particularly interesting is not just the record total; it is how much each match is worth and how the payouts compare with last season.

How Much Does the ATP Finals Singles Champion Earn?

The maximum singles payout is reserved for a player who completes an undefeated campaign. This requires three round-robin victories, a semifinal win, and a victory in the championship match.

The participation fee is adjusted according to the number of group matches a player completes. An alternate who does not enter the competition receives $156,000.

This structure means that a player who wins all three group matches earns $1.553 million before the semifinals. Even if that player loses in the last four, the amount already earned remains theirs.

The doubles competition also offers a substantial financial reward, although the figures are paid per team rather than per individual player.

An undefeated doubles champion pair can earn $959,300. The breakdown includes a $134,200 participation fee for completing all three group matches, $96,600 for each round-robin victory, $178,500 for winning the semifinal and $356,800 for taking the final.

An alternate doubles team receives $51,700.

Alcaraz and Zverev Guaranteed $2.75 Million, With $5.17 Million at Stake in Final

Both finalists have already secured a substantial payday after completing an unbeaten round-robin campaign and winning their respective semifinals.

Since each has won all four matches played so far, Alcaraz and Zverev are guaranteed at least $2,759,000 each, regardless of Sunday's result. This includes the $338,000 participation fee, $1.215 million from their three group-stage victories and the $1.206 million semifinal-winning bonus.

However, the winner will receive an additional $2.412 million for claiming the championship. That would take the total earnings to $5,171,000, making either player the highest-paid singles competitor at this year's tournament.

The runner-up will finish with $2,759,000. Both finalists are also competing for the maximum 1,500 ATP ranking points available at the event.

What Is Different About the Prize Money This Year?

The biggest change in 2026 is the tournament's record-breaking overall purse. The total prize money has increased to $15.75 million, compared with $15.5 million in 2025 (a rise of $250,000).

The maximum singles champion's payout has also increased from $5.071 million in 2025 to $5.171 million this year. That is an additional $100,000 for an undefeated champion.

The doubles payout, however, has remained unchanged from the previous edition. The undefeated winning team will again share $959,300.

There is another major incentive beyond the financial rewards: ATP ranking points. Players receive 200 points for each round-robin victory, 400 for a semifinal win and 500 for winning the final.

An undefeated singles champion can therefore collect a maximum of 1,500 ranking points. Unlike most ATP Tour tournaments, the ATP Finals does not award ranking points simply for participating.

With a record prize pool, valuable ranking points and the distinction of finishing the season as champion, the Turin tournament remains one of the most lucrative prizes in men's tennis.

title: Daniil Medvedev downplays Alexander Zverev’s improvement after ATP Finals defeat
article_text:
Alexander Zverev is one win away from completing his perfect season after he stormed into the championship match at the ATP Finals with a win against Daniil Medvedev.

Zverev recorded his 69th win of a year that has seen him win his first two Grand Slam titles at the Roland Garros and the US Open, with his 7-6(0), 6-4 win over Medvedev in Turin giving him a shot at Carlos Alcaraz in the final.

The newly crowned world No 1 has been frustrated by constant suggestions that he has only claimed the world No 1 ranking due to long-term injuries afflicting Jannik Sinner and Alcaraz.

Medvedev had a 14-8 winning record against Zverev prior to their latest meeting, so he is perfectly placed to give a verdict on whether the German has raised his level over the last year.

Zverev did not face a break point in the two sets against Medvedev, with his opponent suggesting his biggest weapon will always be his serve.

“I think his serve is better,” declared Medvedev, before he was asked if Zverev’s forehand has also gone up a level and he replied: “I will put it this way: I think his forehand was very good even before, and then sometimes he can miss. Today he also missed a couple, so I would not say it’s better.

“I said even before the match, serve is important. Actually, probably Sascha didn’t get broken yet this tournament, so not easy. Didn’t get a break point, so of course not that easy.

“On the tiebreak, I had to do a bit better if I wanted to win the set, and same on the second set when I got broken. Could have done maybe a little bit better. But deserved to lose, so we move on.”

Zverev will be desperate to record a win against Alcaraz and banish the notion that he is a step behind what some have claimed are the real ‘Big 2’ in men’s tennis, with former world No 1 Jim Courier among those admitting outside factors will always cloud some judgements on the German.

Back in June 2024, criminal proceedings against Zverev over allegations he pushed and strangled his ex-girlfriend, Brenda Patea, were discontinued by a Berlin court following a settlement.

Zverev denied the accusations, and court proceedings ended without a verdict or a finding of guilt. Under the agreement, Zverev was ordered to pay €150,000 to the German state and a further €50,000 to charitable organisations.

In an interview with L’Equipe after his Roland Garros victory in June, Zverev said the allegations against him “have been proven false” and that his “innocence has been proven”.

According to Bounces, Patea has filed a new civil lawsuit against Zverev over alleged ‘false statements’ made in that L’Equipe interview, with Courier arguing those allegations will always haunt Zverev.

Want more from Tennis365? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for tennis coverage you can trust.

“Well, the computer is the computer. It doesn’t have any feelings. It just spits out the numbers on who did what,” he said on a recent episode of the Off Court with Greg Rusedski podcast as he spoke about the debate over Zverev’s rise to the world No 1 ranking.

“He’s the most accomplished tennis player this year. He’s got the most points in the last 52 weeks and there he’s the 30th person to have that honour. So yes, he’s earned it. And anyone who doesn’t think that it is just not using their analytical or critical mind. They’re using their emotions.

“And people have strong feelings about Zverev because of all the on-court issues, off-court issues that he’s dealt with over his career that has made it a little more complicated, I think, for some people to to watch his career.

“If you just look at his performance, two major titles, he’s been ultra consistent, and he is the world number one. And I don’t think it’s disputable that the computer is what it is and the ranking is what it is.”

title: Badminton: Wang Zhiyi sets sights on An Seyoung after ending eight-month title wait with Hong Kong Open triumph
Hong Kong Open: Man/Tee Erase 27-Year Blip
article_text:
Man Wei Chong and Tee Kai Wun ended Malaysia’s 27-year wait for a men’s doubles crown at LI-NING Hong Kong Open 2026 on Sunday, delivering a composed 21-19 21-18 victory over Asian Games champions Daniel Marthin and Leo Rolly Carnando.

In doing so, the pair became the first Malaysians to capture the category since legends Cheah Soon Kit and Yap Kim Hock in 1999.

“I’m very grateful to make this history. It’s an honour to follow in the footsteps of greats,” said Man.

“Today is a good story but we already want to focus on next year. We don’t want to think we are champions and then slow down because next year is an important year for us. So we want to fight even harder.”

Against a pair renowned for explosive power, Man and Tee executed a disciplined tactical blueprint to neutralise the Indonesian threat from the outset.

“Everybody knows Daniel’s smash is crazy so we just didn’t want to make it easy for him to use this weapon,” explained Tee. “We had to push them to put them under pressure a little bit and we did that quite well. I made enough room for Man to kill.”

Man credited his partner’s court command for allowing him to dominate the forecourt.

“He controlled the match pretty well, so I got more opportunities in front of the net and more chances to attack.”

While a mid-season knee injury to Man left the duo short of the points required to qualify for next month’s HSBC BWF World Tour Finals, triumphs at last month’s French Open and now in Hong Kong ensure they close their 2026 campaign with formidable momentum.

Meanwhile, Wang Zhi Yi snapped an eight-month title drought in emphatic fashion, cruising past Pornpawee Chochuwong 21-16 21-11 in the women’s singles final.

The victory marks Wang’s first trophy since March – when she stunned the standout An Se Young to claim the All England title – and provides an ideal confidence boost before she heads home to Hangzhou for the World Tour Finals.

“I feel so proud of myself. Today I tried to stay focused and follow my game plan. I’m happy almost like when I won in March,” said Wang.

“It’s a process to always try to keep improving myself. This title means a lot to me. It gives me a lot of confidence to continue my work.”

title: Hong Kong Open — Antonsen declared men’s singles winner after walkover; Zhiyi defends women’s crown
article_text:
Anders Antonsen was declared the men’s singles champion at the Hong Kong Open 2026 after second seed Kunlavut Vitidsarn withdrew from the summit clash with an injury.

“Men’s singles second seed Kunlavut Vitidsarn has withdrawn from his LI-NING Hong Kong Open 2026 final match due to a back injury. His opponent Anders Antonsen will be awarded the title during the prize presentation ceremony,” BWF said in a statement on Sunday.

Antonsen had booked his spot in the final with a commanding 21-13, 21-13 win over India’s Lakshya Sen, while Vitidsarn had gotten the better of Indonesia’s Moh. Zaki Ubaidillah 18-21, 21-15, 21-16 in a 72-minute semifinal battle.

The title in Hong Kong was Antonsen’s second BWF 500 title of the year, having clinched the Thailand Open in May. His opponent in the final then was also Vitidsarn, but the Dane had won the clash in the third game.

In the women’s singles final, two-time Asian Champion Wang Zhiyi defended her title with a dominant win over Pornpawee Chochuwong. Zhiyi took the first game 21-16 before sealing the contest 21-11 in the second game in just 40 minutes.

In the men’ doubles, the Malaysian pair of Man Wei Chong and Tee Kai Wun, who had beaten India’s Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty, went on to beat Indonesia’s Leo Rolly-Daniel Marthin in a tense final.

Wei Chong and Kai Wun won the first game 21-19, with neither pair looking to give away easy points. In the second game, the Malaysian duo pulled away to 16-9 and survived a late surge to seal the contest 21-18.

title: Kunlavut withdraws from Hong Kong Open final with back injury
article_text:
HONG KONG — 22 November 2026, Thailand’s world No. 2 men’s singles badminton player Kunlavut Vitidsarn withdrew from the Hong Kong Open 2026 final due to a back injury, handing the championship title to Denmark’s Anders Antonsen.

The Badminton World Federation (BWF) confirmed the withdrawal on its official Facebook page ahead of Sunday’s scheduled men’s singles final.

Kunlavut, nicknamed “View”, had been due to face Antonsen, the world No. 3, in the championship match.

However, the Thai shuttler was unable to compete because of a back injury, resulting in Antonsen being awarded the title without playing the final.

Kunlavut finished as runner-up at the BWF World Tour Super 500 tournament.

Further details about the severity of his injury and his expected return to competition were not provided in the report.

title: Wei Chong-Kai Wun sign off season in style with Hong Kong Open glory [WATCH]
article_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Man Wei Chong-Tee Kai Wun signed off the season in style by winning their second World Tour men's doubles title at the Hong Kong Open on Sunday.

The Malaysian world No. 9 pair secured a 21-19, 21-18 win over Asian Games champions Leo Rolly Carnando-Daniel Marthin of Indonesia in the Super 500 final at Kai Tak Arena.

It was the French Open champions' second victory in three meetings against world No. 18 Leo Rolly-Daniel.

Wei Chong-Kai Wun's eighth World Tour title earned them US$39,500 (RM162,500), while Leo Rolly-Daniel had to settle for US$19,000 (RM78,200).

Meanwhile, Malaysia are on course for a double triumph as world No. 4 Pearly Tan-M. Thinaah take on Japan's world No. 11 pair Sumire Nakade-Miyu Takahashi in the women's doubles final later on Sunday.

title: Scottie Scheffler, Cameron Young and Wyndham Clark headline PGA Tour Player of the Year award nominees
article_text:
The PGA Tour on Tuesday announced nominees for the two major awards it hands out each year, Player of the Year and Rookie of the Year. Scottie Scheffler, Cameron Young, Wyndham Clark, Matt Fitzpatrick and Chris Gotterup make up the five-man race for the Jack Nicklaus Award, while Alex Fitzpatrick, Ben James, Kristoffer Reitan, Jackson Koivun and Marco Penge are among those vying for the Arnold Palmer Award.

Scheffler has become familiar with getting his hands on the Jack Nicklaus Award in recent years. The world No. 1 joined Tiger Woods as the only golfer to claim the title three years in a row when he secured the honor in 2024. After winning it again in 2025, Scheffler can join Woods again as the only players to ever win it five times in a row. The 15-time major champion won the award five straight seasons from 1999-2003 and three straight from 2005-07.

In 2024, Scheffler became the third golfer to be named Player of the Year three times in his career, joining Woods (11 times) and Rory McIlroy (three). He surpassed McIlroy -- who is not nominated for the award for the first time since the 2020-21 season -- by winning the award again last season.

Scheffler's campaign for a fifth straight Nicklaus award appeared in doubt as he went through the PGA Tour regular season with just one victory. He made up for lost time in the postseason by winning the St. Jude Championship and the Tour Championship for his second career FedEx Cup crown.

The 30-year-old finished inside the top 10 in three of the four major championships, had the lowest scoring average on the PGA Tour and missed only one cut this season.

Scheffler's season was one highlighted by consistency, while Clark's was one of memorable achievements. Clark fired a final-round 60 at The CJ Cup Byron Nelson for the first win of his year before grabbing his second career U.S. Open victory at Shinnecock Hills, with Scheffler by his side on that fateful Sunday.

The wins by Scheffler in the FedEx Cup Playoffs sandwiched a win by Clark at the BMW Championship as he got the better of McIlroy in St. Louis.

Clark and Scheffler's win total of three were matched by both Fitzpatrick and Gotterup. Fitzpatrick won the Valspar Championship before edging out Scheffler in a playoff at the RBC Heritage the week after the Masters. The Englishman was not done, however, and scored the biggest win of his season at the Zurich Classic where he helped secure a PGA Tour card for his little brother Alex.

Meanwhile, Gotterup got off to the hottest start with wins at the Sony Open and the WM Phoenix Open. The big-hitting right hander added another at the John Deere Classic to polish off a transformational season.

Gotterup paired up nicely with Young at the Presidents Cup, one year after Young notched his first win on the PGA Tour. He added to his tally in 2026 with wins at The Players Championship and the Cadillac Championship amid a stretch in the spring where he was the hottest player in the world.

The Rookie of the Year race will be just as compelling given the influx of young talent on the PGA Tour in 2026. Five players are in the running with four of them notching victories, including Penge who claimed the season-finale at the RSM Classic to maintain his playing privileges on the PGA Tour in a season where he dealt with injury.

His fellow Englishman, Fitzpatrick, won the Zurich Classic with his brother, Matt, and went onto collect six top-10 finishes in a limited run on the PGA Tour. One of those finishes came at the Truist Championship where Fitzpatrick fell just short to Reitan, who captured the biggest win of any rookie on the PGA Tour in 2026.

Reitan won the signature event at Quail Hollow Club and also had a top-10 finish at The Memorial Tournament. While the Europeans fared well early in the season, the Americans brought the excitement late with Koivun winning the 3M Open in his third start as a professional. The highly touted amateur got the better of Scheffler at TPC Twin Cities to earn the trophy.

Koivun did not have enough rounds to qualify for a scoring average on the PGA Tour in 2026 where James ranks second only to Scheffler. The No. 1 from PGA Tour University started his career at the Canadian Open and has not looked back as all five of his top-10 finishes also doubled as top-five efforts, including his playoff loss at the World Wide Technology Championship.

The honors will be awarded through a voting process, including PGA Tour members who played in at least 15 official FedEx Cup events during the 2026 season. Voting closes on Friday, Dec. 4 with winners announced at a later date.

title: LIV Golf Creditors Threaten Chapter 7 Liquidation Over $2M Offer
article_text:
LIV Golf’s Chapter 11 bankruptcy case in New Jersey is at risk of being converted to a Chapter 7 liquidation process.

The official committee of unsecured creditors in LIV’s case does not support the current wind-down plan, which is offering just $2 million for general recovery claims. “At present, the plan only benefits the debtors’ current and former directors and officers and the Public Investment Fund of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” the committee wrote in a statement and reservation of rights filed Monday evening.

A Dec. 4 deadline has been set by the creditors and LIV to reach a deal or “immediately move to convert these cases to Chapter 7 and conduct an orderly liquidation of their assets.” In the meantime, settlement negotiations between all parties are underway. The creditors committee did not object to conditional approval of LIV’s revised disclosure statement and wind-down plan, which was granted by Judge Michael Kaplan on Tuesday morning.

If the case converts from Chapter 11 to Chapter 7, LIV’s management team would lose control of proceedings, and a court-appointed trustee would take control of the bankruptcy estate. The Saudi PIF is LIV’s largest creditor, since the nearly $500 million of funding it gave the league to finish the 2026 season came in the form of a secured loan. The sovereign wealth fund put up $49.6 million in debtor-in-possession (DIP) financing to fund the bankruptcy process, and is funding the $2 million being offered to unsecured creditors.

A major concern for the committee is the $2 million being offered for unsecured claims. “At consideration levels that low, the committee believes that unsecured creditors would be better off in a Chapter 7 liquidation,” its statement read. “Given the strength of the claims against PIF and the size of the claims pool—which may exceed $1 billion—any consensual resolution of these cases will require PIF to considerably increase the PIF cash consideration.” The committee also noted that the $2 million pot “would yield materially less than one cent on the dollar in terms of recoveries for general unsecured creditors.”

LIV is arguing Chapter 7 would be worse for everyone involved, though. “We think it would destroy value for all parties,” Matthew Williams, one of LIV’s attorneys from Gibson Dunn, said during Tuesday’s virtual hearing. “The debtors believe that Chapter 7 will leave unsecured creditors worse off, and we don’t think it serves the PIF either.”

The creditors committee is represented by New York–based law firm Willkie Farr & Gallagher and New Jersey–based Fox Rothschild. “We look forward to the continued good-faith negotiations amongst all the parties,” Willkie partner Jim Burbage said Tuesday. “And while there is a lot of wood to chop before we get to a deal, we do remain optimistic that the parties will be able to reach a consensual resolution in the relatively near term.”

Creditors in LIV’s case range from the league’s former star players like Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau—who are owed millions of dollars—to various other contractors and vendors who say they remain unpaid for work they provided for LIV.

Dec. 3 is the next scheduled hearing date in LIV’s bankruptcy case.

title: Tiger Woods 'Melting' The Ball Ahead Of Comeback As Justin Thomas Splits With Caddie: This Week In Golf
article_text:
This Week In Golf: Our regular look at key stories in the game you might have missed as well as other important details you need to know from around the world.

The PGA Tour season has drawn to a conclusion following Marco Penge's dramatic RSM Classic victory, so what's going on this week?

We have a new and highly anticipated DP World Tour season starting Down Under, the return of the Skins Game, the Ladies European Tour finale and much more.

In this edition of This Week In Golf, we'll take you through the latest news and give you all the info you need to know about what's going on in the professional golf world this week. Starting with a certain Tiger Woods...

Tiger Woods is set to return to PGA Tour action next week for the first time since the 2024 Open, having had further injury setbacks and then another high profile car accident in recent times.

The Californian golfing great, now 50, will tee it up in the Hero World Challenge in The Bahamas and progress reports are already filtering out in the media.

No Laying Up's Tron Carter said Woods is reportedly 'melting' the golf ball and carrying bunkers at 320-325 yards per someone who played with him recently.

Subscribe to the Golf Monthly newsletter to stay up to date with all the latest tour news, equipment news, reviews, head-to-heads and buyer’s guides from our team of experienced experts.

It's getting fans excited for the great man's return, and a further podcast report came from Barstool Sports' Fore Play Pod, which said Woods has been doing three-mile incline walks each day to get his fitness back to where it needs to be.

Woods will almost certainly play in the PNC Championship next month, too, where he and son Charlie will be the headline team. All being well, we can expect to see him play a number of times on the main tour, Champions Tour and the Majors next year.

Justin Thomas has split with caddie Matt Minister after nearly two seasons together.

The two-time PGA Champion will have a friend, Brad Gehl, on the bag for the upcoming Skins Game and is hiring Michael Cromie for the 2027 season according to Golfweek.

Thomas and Minister did not manage a victory together since teaming up at the 2024 Masters, as the American won the RBC Heritage with stand-in looper Joe Greiner.

Cromie previously worked with Chris Kirk and also stepped in for Ted Scott at the 2025 BMW Championship and went on to win alongside Scottie Scheffler - bagging $360,000 in the process.

One of the most highly anticipated DP World Tour seasons in recent memory gets underway this week in Sydney at the BMW Australian PGA Championship.

David Puig defends his title in a strong field featuring the likes of Cameron Smith, Adam Scott, Min Woo Lee, Lucas Herbert and a number of DPWT regulars and ex-LIV Golfers.

The Lakes GC hosts the event ahead of next week's Australian Open at Kingston Heath, which will feature Rory McIlroy.

It will be the first of 42 tournaments on the schedule in 24 countries, which includes the return of the Singapore Open, Portugal Open and Hong Kong Open. This week's tournament features an AUD $2.5m prize fund.

The former Ripper GC captain is one of nine players to have agreed DPWT sponsor invite deals for 2027, and he admitted his goal is to make his way back to the PGA Tour.

"I guess that's the path. That's where I want to be now for sure," Smith told the Australian Associated Press.

"DP's given us a chance to kind of fulfil that. We'll see how that goes. There's plenty of good players out there and plenty of other guys that want to do the same thing, so it's going to be difficult.

"But for sure that's where I want to play.

"I think given what they've told me, I pretty much need to win this year to get membership.

"It's all still very blurry to me at the moment. There are a lot of rules, but we'll have a few opportunities, and like I said, I've always managed to play pretty good down here, so why not start it off with a good one?"

The Skins Game returns for its second edition since re-launching last year, where Wyndham Clark, Brooks Koepka, Justin Thomas and Jackson Koivun will compete for a share of the $4m purse.

The event takes place on Black Friday, November 27 at 9am ET, and will stream live on Prime Video. Atlantic Fields Club in Hobe Sound, Florida will be the stage, with Andrew Catalon, Colt Knost and Dan Rapaport on the mics.

The rules have changed from last year's 'Reverse Purse' back to a standard format where all four players start at $0. As per usual skins rules, each hole carries a dollar value and tied holes roll over to raise the stakes.

La Cala Resort hosts the Andalucía Costa del Sol Open de España this week on the Ladies European Tour.

The season finale sees a 75-woman field competing over 72-holes with no cut, where the winner will earn €105,000 from the €700,000 prize fund.

Casandra Alexander has already secured the Order of Merit but the Rookie of the Year title is still on the line.

Alexander headlines the field alongside Mimi Rhodes, Anne van Dam, Anna Huang and Ana Peláez Triviño.

title: PGA Tour reveals nominees for 2026 Jack Nicklaus Award, Arnold Palmer Award
article_text:
PONTE VEDRA BEACH, Florida – The PGA Tour announced Tuesday nominees for the Jack Nicklaus Award (Player of the Year) and the Arnold Palmer Award (Rookie of the Year) for the 2026 season as finalized by the PGA Tour Player Directors and members of the Player Advisory Council (PAC).

Five players are nominated for the Jack Nicklaus Award as the 2026 PGA Tour Player of the Year (alphabetically): Wyndham Clark, Matt Fitzpatrick, Chris Gotterup, Scottie Scheffler and Cameron Young. The five nominees for the Arnold Palmer Award as the 2026 PGA Tour Rookie of the Year are Alex Fitzpatrick, Ben James, Jackson Koivun, Marco Penge and Kristoffer Reitan.

The Player of the Year and Rookie of the Year awards are determined by a member vote, with PGA Tour members who played in at least 15 official tournaments during the 2026 season eligible to vote. The voting will close Friday, Dec. 4, at 5 p.m. ET, with the winners announced at a later date.

- Entered 25 events with wins (three) at THE CJ CUP Byron Nelson, U.S. Open and BMW Championship

- No. 5 in the Official World Golf Ranking and No. 21 in the FedExCup

- Ranked third on Tour in Putting Average (1.698) and eighth in Bounce Back Percentage (28.29%)

- No. 3 in the Official World Golf Ranking and No. 21 in the FedExCup

- Ranked inside the top 10 on Tour in SG: Approach the Green (10th/.605), SG: Around the Green (second/.494) and SG: Total (second/1.359)

- No. 7 in the Official World Golf Ranking and No. 4 in the FedExCup

- Ranked third on Tour in Driving Distance – All Drives (309.2)

- Entered 20 events with wins (three) at The American Express, FedEx St. Jude Championship and Tour Championship

- No. 1 in the Official World Golf Ranking and claimed the FedExCup title

- Winner of the Byron Nelson Award for Low Scoring Average (68.619)

- No. 4 in the Official World Golf Ranking and No. 11 in the FedExCup

- Ranked ninth on Tour in SG: Tee-to-Green (1.092) second in Round 2 Scoring Average (67.90)

- One of two rookies to qualify for the Tour Championship and finished No. 4 in the FedExCup

- Made 12 cuts in 14 starts and finished No. 53 in the FedExCup Fall standings

- Earned PGA Tour membership as the No. 1 player in the 2026 PGA Tour University Ranking

- Made 10 cuts in 12 starts and finished No. 67 in the FedExCup Fall standings

- Made 15 cuts in 22 starts and finished No. 64 in the FedExCup Fall standings

- One of two rookies to qualify for the Tour Championship and finished No. 25 in the FedExCup

A player’s rookie season is defined as the season in which he becomes a PGA Tour member and plays in 10 or more events as a member or finishes in the top 100 in the FedExCup standings or qualifies as a top 70 non-member, whichever occurs first. A new member who previously played in more than seven official PGA Tour money events as a professional in a prior season is not eligible for PGA Tour Rookie of the Year.

title: David Lipsky falls out of top 100, Marco Penge soars in during dramatic FedExCup Fall finale
article_text:
ST. SIMONS ISLAND, Ga. – The PGA Tour season ended with no shortage of drama.

For the second consecutive week, a Tour event needed a Monday finish, and this time, 72 holes weren't enough to crown a champion. The RSM Classic came down to the Tour's first four-man playoff since the 2015 Greenbrier Classic, with more than a tournament title hanging in the balance.

Players spent the final round moving in and out of the top 100 in the FedExCup Fall standings, fighting to secure full status for 2027. When the dust settled, only two players had crossed the all-important threshold.

Marco Penge delivered the biggest move, climbing from No. 120 to No. 64 after birdieing the first playoff hole to claim his maiden PGA Tour title. David Lipsky, meanwhile, fell from No. 97 to No. 102 after missing the cut, leaving him with conditional status for next season.

Then there was John Parry, who walked off the Seaside Course on Friday believing he had lost his card. Instead, he survived a weekend of leaderboard movement to finish at No. 100, claiming the final spot for full status in 2027.

Here's a closer look at the players who moved across the bubble and where other notable names finished in the FedExCup Fall finale.

- Marco Penge (FedExCup Fall No. 120, projected No. 64)

Penge arrived at Sea Island Golf Club needing at least a two-way tie for fourth to crack the top 100. He left with far more than a PGA Tour card.

Returning to the 18th for the first extra hole, Penge delivered another precise wedge shot and made birdie to secure his first PGA Tour victory. The win earned him an exemption through 2027, spots in The Players Championship, The Sentry and the PGA Championship, plus a spot in the Tour's inaugural season of the Championship Series in 2028.

For Penge, winning wasn't necessarily the objective when the week began. Keeping his card was.

"The start of this week, my goal was to get into the top 100, and then felt like it was so stressful day by day, shot by shot. (I was) just trying to make sure I didn't do anything stupid," Penge said. "I'm kind of prone to hitting a wild tee shot here and there, so I was trying to keep it on the straight and narrow."

He did just that, missing only one fairway during Monday's final round.

With his playing privileges on the line, Penge initially approached the day with caution. But as the round progressed and his position inside the top 100 became more secure, his focus shifted from protecting his card to chasing the trophy.

"I felt like once I got through maybe nine holes today, I felt that I was going to be OK," Penge said. "Maybe for 14 holes I thought, OK, I've got a chance where I can actually win this. Then I kind of changed my mindset all of a sudden and tried to birdie every hole coming in. Luckily, I just did enough to get into a playoff and got it over the line."

The victory was another defining moment for Penge, who had previously navigated a similar fight to retain his status on the DP World Tour. This time, he emerged with a title and renewed confidence in his ability to perform when the stakes are highest.

"I proved to myself I can do it under the most immense pressure," Penge said. "I always seem to play my best golf when my back's up against the wall. I've been through this before on the DP World Tour, keeping my card in the last event and dealing with adversity and coming back from health issues, all that stuff. So I knew I could do it, I just wasn't sure I ever had the game this week to be able to do it, and thankfully I did."

- David Lipsky (FedExCup Fall No. 97, projected No. 102)

Lipsky entered The RSM inside the top 100 but will have to settle for conditional status in 2027 after missing the cut by two shots at Sea Island. He made 15 cuts in 25 starts this season, highlighted by a runner-up finish at the Valspar Championship.

- John Parry (FedExCup Fall No. 96, projected No. 100)

Few players endured a more anxious weekend than Parry, whose missed cut left his future on Tour in the hands of others.

A three-putt on his final hole Friday at the Seaside Course brought the Englishman to tears, believing he had squandered his chance to retain full status. With no more golf left to play, all he could do was watch.

As the final two rounds unfolded, Parry's projected position fluctuated above and below the top-100 cutline. Ultimately, the results fell his way, leaving him at No. 100 and securing the final full-status spot for 2027.

The Belgian fell short of the top 100 but made a significant move toward securing playing opportunities for next season. Four rounds in the 60s (68-66-68-67) earned Dumont de Chassart a tie for seventh, his best finish of 2026, and lifted him inside the top 125 for conditional status in 2027.

Sea Island once again brought out the best in McGreevy, who followed last year's runner-up finish with a tie for 10th. But despite another strong showing, the 31-year-old Oklahoma native couldn't climb high enough in the standings to secure full status.

title: High Time: How Craig Kessler and his ‘scrappy’ team are putting LPGA back together
article_text:
NAPLES, Fla. – Craig Kessler is running out of time.

It’s Tuesday morning ahead of the LPGA’s season finale, the CME Group Tour Championship, and the second-year commissioner has less than 15 minutes until his 9 a.m. pro-am tee time, he’s yet to hit balls, and to top it all off, his cart is nowhere to be found. Not that Kessler is fretting, even with the first hole a few hundred yards away.

With one strap of his carry bag slung over his shoulder, he calmly strolls to the range, where he strikes about a dozen balls, mostly wedges, and then heads to the tee, still on foot.

Ironically enough, Kessler arrives to find his cart waiting for him, but less than a hole into Kessler’s round, he ditches it anyway to walk with his playing partners, which include LPGA veteran Jenny Shin and executives from Ford and American Express. Kessler later suggests to the group that maybe all pro-ams should be cart-less for the sake of better conversation. He’s not wrong.

Over the next several hours, the 41-year-old Kessler provides a masterclass in personability. The storytelling in the group is so good that Shin, on a few occasions, must remind her caddie he still has a job to do. When she and two of the amateurs pour in three 30-plus-footers on top of each other on the third green, Kessler quips, “Want to take the magnet out of the bottom of the cup now?”

As his first full season winds down, Kessler, the man, is already proving himself a force.

But what about Kessler, the leader? While the LPGA has some nice wins already in the Kessler era, its boss isn’t satisfied.

“I’m so proud of what the team has accomplished this year,” Kessler says. “I’m thrilled with the progress we’re making but clear-eyed about how much work we still have to do.”

A glass of red wine in hand, Kessler makes the rounds inside The Ritz-Carlton’s lobby bar on Wednesday night, conversing with his employees, sponsors and random guests who are probably shocked to be chatting with someone of Kessler’s standing.

Before that, Kessler had just spent a couple hours at a media reception, usually the type of function where execs can’t wait to dip, especially considering the day’s itinerary. Kessler started with a 9 a.m. state-of-the-tour press conference, then attended an LPGA Foundation board meeting before his 10-minute spot just after noontime on Golf Channel’s “Golf Central,” which is airing the first of five hours before a shot is even hit in the $11 million tournament. He has a few sit-downs as well. In between obligations, he catches up with his wife, high-school sweetheart Nicole, who offers words of encouragement.

By Thursday morning, Kessler is up early and in the hotel café, still energized and eager to chat.

It’s a stark contrast to Kessler’s predecessor, Molly Marcoux Samaan, who often struggled to work the room.

Under Samaan, the LPGA saw a significant increase in prize money. Major purses more than doubled. The winner’s check at the season-ending CME ballooned to $4 million. But the tour otherwise remained stagnant at best, losing viewership, sponsors and perhaps most importantly, the trust of the players. Operational and communication gaffes such as the shuttle crisis at the 2024 Solheim Cup only raised the temperature underneath Samaan’s hotseat, until Samaan resigned in December 2024, less than five years into her post.

The common opinion about Samaan is that she failed to inspire, both internally and externally.

“They say it takes a village, and I think their village is getting a little fractured,” Terry Duffy, CEO of CME Group, told Golfweek back in 2022 after not a single player attended a sponsor dinner the Tuesday evening of the season finale.

Kessler heard as much during his interview process.

“I probably talked to dozens of people … and the theme that kept surfacing was the importance of building trust,” Kessler said. “The organization certainly had some scar tissue, so building trust was priority No. 1, trust with the players, sponsors, staff.”

Before Kessler, then the COO of the PGA of America, signed his contract, he met one on one with a few of the LPGA’s biggest names, knowing he needed their buy-in. After more than 200 days on the road, the father of three boys has earned it.

“He’s always asking what we can do better but also what is going well,” said Hannah Green, one of the LPGA’s player directors. “He’s always enthusiastic about trying to make this place better, and perhaps we haven’t had that in the past. I think Mike [Whan, now CEO at the USGA] was a great leader. I never worked with Molly, but I feel like sometimes people get the short end of the stick and they’ve got nothing to really work with.”

Said fellow player director Lauren Coughlin: “Every time I hear him talk in any kind of big setting, I’m just very impressed by him. He’s great with people. He’s so smart. I just don’t know how he keeps it all in his head. It’s crazy sitting in a board meeting and he doesn’t even have like a ton of notes or anything.”

Added veteran Alison Lee: “It seems like he cares so much about every single player on this tour. … He does a really good job showing us that as well, so it makes us feel heard. It makes us feel like we can go to him whenever we want.”

title: LPGA Tour card blow for Gemma Dryburgh at end of Q-Series
article_text:
Gemma Dryburgh has lost her seat at the LPGA Tour’s top table for the first time since 2018 after having to settle for Epson Tour status at the end of the circuit’s Q-Series.

The Aberdonian, who landed a maiden victory in the TOTO Japan Classic in 2022, finished joint-47th in the five-round card battle at RJT Trail at Magnolia Grove in Mobile, Alabama.

The top 25 and ties secured Category 15 cards for the 2027 LPGA Tour season, with all the other players completing at least four rounds earning Epson Tour status.

Dryburgh, who played in the 2023 Solheim Cup in Spain, found herself involved in this year’s Q-Series after finishing 114th in the 2026 Race to CME Globe Ranking on the LPGA Tour.

In the same position in 2021, she finished T22 to hang on to her card for the main tour before going on to claim 45th spot on the money–list the following season then a career-best 41st in 2023.

She slipped to 70th last season and will now be bitterly disappointed to have ended her first year playing as a new mum on a low note.

South African Casandra Alexander, this year’s LET Order of Merit winner, was among a total of 27 players to secure LPGA Tour cards for next season.

Meanwhile, Lorna McClymont will go straight to the final stage in the upcoming LET Lalla Aicha Qualifying School in Morocco through finishing 18th in this season’s LET Access Series Order of Merit.

Hannah Darling, Louise Duncan, Gabrielle Macdonald, Taylor White, Laura Beveridge, Alison Muirhead, Kimberley Beveridge, Kirsty Mitchell and Summer Elliott all face First Stage tests on 10-12 December, also in Morocco.

title: These 8 big names just lost their PGA Tour card
article_text:
Marco Penge was 120th in the FedEx Cup rankings heading into one of the biggest weeks of his career at the RSM Classic. It seemed the Englishman was going to be among the most surprising names to lose their PGA Tour card.

But Penge has a habit of delivering when under the gun. Two years after salvaging his DP World Tour card with a gutsy finish in Korea, Penge not only did enough to keep his playing rights in America, but he claimed his first PGA Tour title.

After a ‘nightmare’ season derailed by personal health and family issues, Penge saved his best until last with a five-under 65 on the rain-delayed final day, forcing his way into a four-man playoff. He birdied the first extra playoff hole to win a $1.3million prize and, crucially, secure his place in the lucrative PGA Tour Championship Series from 2028.

There was another English success story, too. John Parry, who missed the cut after a disastrous three-putt on his closing hole, somehow clung on to the 100th and final card after an agonising weekend wait.

Only the top 100 golfers after the FedEx Cup Fall Series secured their full cards for next year, while the top 125 are given conditional status and starts into certain events.

But for every John Parry there was a story of woe and regret. Here are the notable and surprising names who have lost their PGA Tour card…

A brutal end to what was so nearly an uplifting start to his PGA Tour career. The likeable Dane made 18 cuts in 24 starts this year, but he slipped down the leaderboard at the RSM Classic on Monday and narrowly misses out on full playing rights.

It could have been so different for Li. He was part of the four-man playoff won by Penge and had chances to win the tournament. But he will now mix his time between the PGA Tour and the DP World Tour next season.

Horschel returned from hip surgery in May 2025 and played a full schedule, but graded his 31-event season an ‘F’. The former FedEx Cup champ was not all doom and gloom though as he still retains conditional status. “I know I’m going to get in quite a few events and I’ve got to be able to take advantage of those opportunities,” he said.

The 2025 European Ryder Cup player had a torrid run, withdrawing from both the Biltmore Championship and the Butterfield Bermuda Championship, while missing the cut at the Bank of Utah Championship. But it all looked entirely salvageable as Hojgaard held the lead at the RSM Classic. He headed into the final round needing a tie for third for survival, but only managed T5 as he stumbled to the finish line. He will still make some PGA Tour starts, but right now Hojgaard looks to be the most likely dispensable from the winning team at Bethpage as we approach another Ryder Cup year.

It seemed inconceivable that the 2009 US Open champion would lose his card, especially after the renaissance that saw him win twice in a matter of weeks three years ago. But the 47-year-old’s age caught up with him during an abject year where he failed to capitalize on his position in Signature Events.

The Full Swing star had a mini-revival after appearing overawed on the PGA Tour. The two-time Korn Ferry Tour winner had a horrific start to the season and two top-10 finishes in the fall came too late.

Before Jackson Koivun, Blades Brown and Ben James it was Luke Clanton who was supposed to be America’s next superstar. That of course could still transpire, but this was a year when the youngster went backwards. Clanton made transition to the top table look seamless as a college player, threatening the leaders numerous times as an amateur. But in the paid ranks he’s struggled only made half of his cuts this season.

Dahmen was in contention at Torrey Pines at the start of the season before he was blown away by Justin Rose. Back in February, it seemed the lovable American had something to build on. But it has been a struggle since for Dahmen, who only just missed out on conditional status via the top 125.

title: For sure I want to return to the PGA Tour, says ex-LIV Golf player Cameron Smith
article_text:
SYDNEY – Australian Cameron Smith has moved on from LIV Golf, is preparing for his invitation-only appearances on the DP World Tour and is already thinking about a return to the PGA Tour.

As the 2022 British Open champion prepared for the Australian PGA Championship starting on Nov 26 at The Lakes in Sydney, attention inevitably turned to his career goals and his steps toward a possible return to the PGA Tour.

“I guess that’s the path. That’s where I want to be now for sure,” the 33-year-old told the Australian Associated Press. “DP’s given us a chance to kind of fulfil that. We’ll see how that goes. There’s plenty of good players out there and plenty of other guys that want to do the same thing, so it’s going to be difficult.

“But for sure that’s where I want to play.”

Currently, the top 10 from the European tour’s “Race to Dubai” season points list qualify for the PGA Tour. To even have a chance at that, Smith needs to play more tournaments on the DP World Tour’s 2027 schedule.

He could do that by winning the co-sanctioned Australian PGA Championship for a fourth time or the Dec 3-6 Australian Open at Kingston Heath, which also features world No. 2 Rory McIlroy.

“I think given what they’ve told me, I pretty much need to win this year to get membership,” Smith said. “It’s all still very blurry to me at the moment. There’s a lot of rules, but we’ll have a few opportunities and like I said, I’ve always managed to play pretty good down here, so why not start it off with a good one?”

The PGA Tour board last week said it had “thoughtful discussions” about the future of players at LIV Golf but otherwise seemed to be in no hurry to decide if there is room for them next season.

CEO Brian Rolapp said the “returning member programme” that allowed Brooks Koepka to return to the PGA Tour in 2026 with financial penalties was not on the table.

Smith did not take up that one-time offer in January, which applied only to players who had won Majors or The Players Championship from 2022 till 2025.

So he is in a kind of limbo. LIV Golf, which lost the financial support of Saudi Arabia and filed for bankruptcy on Sept 8, told a bankruptcy court earlier in November it had abandoned plans for a new version of the league and had begun winding down its business.

“There was a lot of uncertainty and then in a way it was good to just like get the noise over and done with,” Smith said. “It was a big move to go to LIV at the start for sure, and I think everyone that was close to me and all my friends saw why I was doing it and why I made the decision.”

Former world No. 1 and 2013 Masters champion Adam Scott said he had no doubts about Smith fitting back in.

“Cam’s incredibly talented and he’ll adjust to his new environment,” the 46-year-old Australian said. “He’ll be just fine.” AP

title: Who's in, who's out? PGA Tour's playing status drama goes down to final putt
2026 LPGA Q-Series Final Qualifying final results: Prize money payout, leaderboard, who earned LPGA status
article_text:
The 2026 LPGA Final Qualifying final leaderboard is headed by winner Megha Ganne, with the American player winning the five-round marathon on the Robert Trent Jones Golf Trail at Magnolia Grove -- the Crossings Course and Falls Course -- in Alabama.

Ganne won the 90-hole event on 23-under total, good enough for a one-shot win over Shannon Tan and Julia Gregg.

In total, 27 players earned LPGA status for 2027. Players finishing in positions 1-25 and ties earned LPGA Tour status in Category 15, giving them entry into most full-field LPGA events. Players who finished outside that top 25 and ties have status on the Epson Tour in 2027 in Category C.

In the final round, which closed on Monday, four players moved from outside the top 25 and ties into the cutoff: Marie Madsen (T-34 to T-15), Maria Fassi (T-46 to T-23), Achiraya Sriwong (T-41 to T-23) and Da Yeon Lee (T-41 to T-23).

The cutoff to get an LPGA card for 2027 was 3-under 283 and better. A total of 114 players from a starting 114 completed the tournament.

Ganne won the $15,000 winner's share of the $150,000 purse.

Final Qualifying is a five-round competition with a cut after 72 holes. Magnolia Grove (Crossings and Falls Courses) hosted the entire event, with the Crossings holding the final round.

This is the latest iteration for Final Qualifying, which had been known as Q-Series and had replaced the third-and-final stage of LPGA Q-School. The final stage was previously eight rounds in the first four years, turning to six last year and a scheduled five for the last two years.

There was a cut after four rounds to the top 65 and ties to make it a little easier to get the field through the difficult final round to maintain status.

title: LIV Golf Secures $2.2 Million From UK Travel Firm as $700,000 Dispute Continues
article_text:
LIV Golf's bankruptcy estate is set to receive approximately $2.2 million from Corporate Travel Management (United Kingdom) Limited following an agreement reached between both parties in the league's ongoing Chapter 11 proceedings.

A consent order filed in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of New Jersey requires the travel services company to transfer the money to LIV Golf's debtors within seven days of the order's entry. The agreement resolves part of a dispute over funds held by the company.

However, approximately $700,000 will remain with Corporate Travel Management while the parties continue to resolve their respective claims. The development was highlighted by David Rumsey, who shared details of the court document on X.

LIV Golf Set to Receive $2.2 Million From Corporate Travel Management

The court order concerns a motion filed by LIV Golf's debtors against Corporate Travel Management (UK) Limited, also known as CTM. The motion sought to enforce the automatic stay, compel the return of debtor funds and impose sanctions against the travel company.

Both parties reached an agreement to resolve the motion without an admission of liability or a court decision on the merits of their respective positions.

Under the terms of the consent order, CTM must transfer approximately $2.2 million to LIV Golf's debtors. The payment must follow written wire instructions provided by the debtors' legal representatives.

The order also states that the transfer will be in full and final satisfaction of all rights and claims between the parties concerning those particular funds. CTM will not be entitled to recover any portion of the transferred money for any reason.

The parties can also agree in writing for some or all of the money to be sent in pounds sterling to a UK account designated by LIV Golf's debtors. The actual amounts transferred in the relevant currencies will determine the payment, rather than the approximate US dollar figure.

However, the order does not mean the entire dispute between LIV Golf and CTM has been settled. The agreement only addresses the funds covered by the $2.2 million transfer.

While CTM has agreed to return approximately $2.2 million, the company is permitted to retain the remaining funds, estimated to be worth around $700,000.

The court order allows CTM to hold the money while the parties' respective rights are determined through the claims-allowance process in LIV Golf's Chapter 11 cases, another appropriate legal proceeding or a further written agreement.

However, CTM cannot transfer, use or otherwise dispose of the retained funds without an order from the court or an agreement with LIV Golf's debtors. Any agreement to release the money must also satisfy the consent requirements involving the debtor-in-possession lender.

Importantly, the court has not decided whether LIV Golf or CTM is entitled to the remaining $700,000. The order also does not allow CTM to use the money to satisfy any claim it may have against the debtors without further court approval or a written agreement.

The latest agreement therefore gives LIV Golf a route to recover approximately $2.2 million while leaving another significant portion of the disputed funds unresolved.

The seven-day transfer requirement will be the next important step, while the remaining $700,000 will continue to depend on the outcome of the parties' claims or a further agreement.

title: Qualifiers for all 2027 Signature Events, The Players and majors
article_text:
Narratives can be prioritized, but just because one attracts more attention than another, it doesn’t mean that it’s less valuable. This is especially evident when it presents as a bonus.

The RSM Classic truly has something for everyone. It’s a PGA Tour stop awarding an official victory that happens to be at the end of a 10-month parade of official victories, but while those who choose to play are chasing that singular carrot, it’s also the moment in time when outcomes of the pursuit of secondary goals are determined. Short of winning the annual tournament at Sea Island Golf Club, a spot inside the top 100 of the FedExCup arguably is the next most impactful.

Marco Penge is in the books as the champion of the 2026 season finale. He birdied the only hole needed in a four-way playoff to outlast also-rans Max Greyserman, Haotong Li and Michael Thorbjornsen. It happened on Monday, not Sunday, this due to a Saturday washout that served more as an extended halftime after the cut fell on Friday.

When Penge’s short try dropped into the cup at the par-4 18th hole in sudden death, he secured exemptions into The Players Championship and the PGA Championship in 2027, as well as a spot in the Championship Series when the PGA Tour evolves into the new two-tier system in 2028. It’s heady stuff for a PGA Tour rookie who arrived for his debut in the Golden Isles slotted 120th in the FedExCup. A performance worthy of a promotion into the top-100 bubble easily would have qualified as a success – he finished 64th – so, he got that but so much more.

For many who didn’t win, what rapidly became Penge’s bonus was their golden ticket, as it were. The top 100 is where fully exempt status ends when using the FedExCup as the measurement. A handful inside (and outside) the top 100 who pegged it at Sea Island already are exempt in 2027 via a victory of their own or for having finished inside the top 70 to qualify for the FedExCup Playoffs, but that cohort stood in stark contrast beside members who were not.

When the dust finally settled on the updated tabulation of the FedExCup, fewer futures were as foggy as they were when The RSM Classic commenced. Snaring a 2027 PGA Tour card is the headline as the primary goal, but it comes with the immediate benefit of a spot in The Players in March. After Penge, another 24 members secured that as well on the extra day of the season.

Criteria are listed in chronological order where possible. Until all are confirmed, best estimates are given and all are subject to change.

- Winners of PGA Tour events through the final week before The Players.

- Top 10 in the FedExCup at the conclusion of the Cognizant Classic in The Palm Beaches (Feb. 28).

- Top 50 of the Official World Golf Ranking (March 1).

title: RSM Classic Full Prize Money Payout 2026
