title: LIV Golf could make shock return as former player reveals intriguing takeover rumour
article_text:
Former LIV Golf player Travis Smyth has claimed the defunct breakaway tour could yet return in the future.

The circuit filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September, and officially collapsed earlier this month after a proposed $300m restructuring deal with a London-based credit firm fell through.

BC Partners Credit had demanded that a minimum number of marquee players sign new contracts by late October to finalise the rescue package, before walking away when several star names opted to leave the tour.

Smyth, 31, played in the inaugural LIV event at Centurion Club in 2022 and made eight further appearances as a reserve - including four starts this season - despite never holding a full-time team contract.

While the Australian did not win an individual title on the circuit, he was part of victorious teams alongside Bryson DeChambeau's Crushers GC in Korea and the all-Australian Ripper GC side in the UK this summer.

Speaking to Fox Sports Australia ahead of this week's Australian PGA Championship at The Lakes in Sydney, Smyth suggested BC Partners head Ted Goldthorpe has not completely abandoned hopes of a revival.

"I still wish it was around," he said. "I loved it. I believed in it. I thought it was great fun as a player.

"Travelling to those countries, it meant that I could be in Sydney, Australia a little bit more. I love that sort of idea. I kind of envisioned that a little bit. But it's gone now. I don't know for what reasons.

"I guess ultimately the bigger players, not enough of them signed up for whatever reason. But hope it comes back.

"Actually I heard a rumour that the leading investor dude, Ted [Goldthorpe], from BC Partners, is still trying to buy it, so it might come back in the future."

Reflecting on his time competing on the circuit, Smyth added: "My experience was amazing, obviously.

"I was playing at the time [on the] Asian Tour, a tour that only feeds into LIV. The only pathway forward. So that's what I was always striving for.

"I'm super grateful that I got to play. On Bryson's team with a win, on Ripper's team with a team win, had a top 10 myself in one of those starts, so it was an amazing experience."

The New South Wales native was also quizzed on LIV's lavish spending. It's understood the Saudi PIF ploughed more than $5bn into the venture.

"I don't even know if the Saudis cared how much they would spend," Smyth said.

"I don't really know if that model being sustainable was even like a concern.

"But from all reports, the way it was going to be next year, was that it was structured to be a sustainable product, and it would have made it work.

"I don't think we'll ever see a golf tour the way that it was before with the Saudis just going all out.

"Because it felt like there was just so much wasted money, so much, just everything going on at those tournaments."

Following the demise of LIV Golf, Smyth has secured playing privileges on the DP World Tour and plans to contest roughly 26 tournaments over the next 12 months.

"Now DP [World Tour] and the Asian Tour have sort of got back together and so over the next 12 months, I'll focus on DP and I'll get to play the co-sanction events in Asia, so I'll get my starts up there," he said.

"I feel like it's all just sort of mixing in perfectly.

"I'll pretty much play every event that I can possibly get into on the DP schedule.

"I'm going to go to Mauritius after Aussie Open.

"Then if I don't get into certain events and there happens to be an Asian Tour event or a Japan Tour event, I might go play.

"But I think my category is going to get a lot of starts in DP and I'm gearing up to play, I don't know, 26 events for the year."

title: Talor Gooch is now facing a very harsh reality as LIV Golf folds
article_text:
It was five years ago this week that Talor Gooch secured his first win on the PGA Tour, as he won The RSM Classic by three shots.

Less than two years later, Gooch was declaring himself one of the best players in the world after a superb season on LIV Golf in which he won three times.

As the 2026 season concludes, however, the 35-year-old finds himself facing an incredibly long road back to the PGA Tour.

And crucially, there are few signs to suggest that he is ready for the challenge.

Gooch is one of the most successful players in LIV Golf history. His four victories helped him earn more than $72 million in prize money.

Nevertheless, he became a figure of ridicule for many of the league’s biggest critics.

There was no shortage of comments made by those associated with LIV Golf that did the league no favours whatsoever during its existence.

But one of the most infamous claims came from Gooch following a LIV event at Pumpkin Ridge in 2022 in which he suggested that the atmosphere was not too dissimilar to what you would see at a Ryder Cup or Presidents Cup.

Of course, it did not help Gooch had played in neither event.

Who do you think will be golf's breakout star in 2027?

The PGA Tour and DP World Tour both look incredibly strong next year!

Meanwhile, in 2023, Gooch claimed that he was one of the best players in the world after clinching the individual title for the season on LIV. In fairness, he had won three times that year, so that comment was a little more understandable.

His status did not help earn him an invite for The Masters the following year. Nevertheless, he went on to hit the headlines for suggesting that there would be an asterisk against Rory McIlroy‘s name if he completed the Career Grand Slam that year at Augusta National due to the fact that some of the best players on LIV were missing from the event.

It should be noted that Gooch has played in six majors since LIV Golf’s first ever event in 2022. He has missed the cut three times and never finished higher than 34th.

He took on a leadership role with LIV at the start of 2026 following Brooks Koepka‘s departure from the league. And his captaincy led to Smash being rebranded as OKGC during the season.

Of course, LIV Golf is now no more. But while many are waiting to see what the future holds for the likes of Bryson DeChambeau, Jon Rahm, Dustin Johnson, and Cam Smith, there appears to be virtually no chatter about what is next for Gooch.

He won four times in total and is third on LIV’s all-time money list. He was apparently one of the best players in the world for a spell.

And yet, you would have been forgiven for not even noticing that he was missing from the list of players who have struck a deal with the DP World Tour for the 2027 season.

Perhaps he will still receive some invites to DP World Tour events next season. But it is seemingly going to be extremely difficult for Gooch to regain his PGA Tour card for 2028 as things stand.

There was undoubtedly a time when Gooch was one of LIV’s biggest success stories. However, the silence concerning what comes next for him may say everything about his current status in the game.

title: Peter Finch's DP World Tour Invite Is Not 'Pathetic'
article_text:
News of Peter Finch's sponsor's invitation into the upcoming AfrAsia Bank Mauritius Open unsurprisingly caused plenty of discussion on social media, and it's perhaps an instant example of how the decision has already been a success.

Golf Monthly's news story has had over 145,000 views on X in just a few days with over 70 replies and quote-tweets, including from the man himself who admitted there had been "quite the range of comments."

The platform formerly known as 'Twitter' is not always regarded as the friendliest of places and, while there was plenty of support for the YouTube giant, there was inevitably some 'hate' dished out following the news of his DP World Tour debut.

The man with over 850,000 subscribers' invite "deprives a hard working pro and his family the chance to earn a living," one user wrote, while there were some harsher calls of "pathetic", "joke" and an "embarrassment."

The news comes amid the European circuit agreeing sponsor invite deals with nine ex-LIV Golfers, so the subject of DP World Tour invites and making life harder for the DPWT rank-and-file is a current topic of significant debate.

A news story on defending champion Jayden Schaper or two-time Masters champion Bubba Watson committing to the event would not have received anywhere near the views, which I think illustrates the struggle certain tournament officials are facing.

The golfing calendar is incredibly packed and it's tough for events like the Mauritius Open to stand out when there's another three or four on in the same week and then another three or four more the next week. That's not to even mention YouTube Golf, Netflix, other sports, streaming and the rest of the internet that tour events are having to compete with.

Subscribe to the Golf Monthly newsletter to stay up to date with all the latest tour news, equipment news, reviews, head-to-heads and buyer’s guides from our team of experienced experts.

The Mauritius Open features one of the most naturally beautiful settings of the season but it has a low purse and a fairly weak field, so Finch's addition has obviously been made to increase eyeballs on what would usually be a fairly missable week.

We've seen YouTubers added to fields before on various global and we'll almost certainly see it again. Luke Kwon, Mac Boucher and 'Taco Golf' received Asian Tour invites, while Brad Dalke made the cut at this year's BMW International Open on the DP World Tour, the same tournament which invited the Bryan Bros last year.

PGA Tour winner, Wesley, was also joined in the field by his brother, George, at the PGA Tour's Bermuda Championship in 2024. The pair also played in last year's International Series Philippines event on the Asian Tour.

So YouTubers being invited is nothing new, and the only thing new here is the man in question. Peter Finch will be making his debut on the DP World Tour and I for one am very much looking forward to tuning in.

Would I have been watching the opening round of the Mauritius Open without his participation? I can't say for sure that I would, and that will be the same for many.

Thursday and Friday tour golf is intriguing but not exactly the most gripping, and having Finch there for at least the first two days will inevitably increase viewership. It will also lead to plenty of social media coverage before the event, too.

A user replied to our post that Finch will likely shoot 78-78 and miss the cut while another stated he "isn't anywhere near good enough." I would like to challenge those as the Englishman undoubtedly has some serious game and has shown plenty of signs in recent years that he can hang with the pros.

Just two months ago, Finch finished T6th in a Tartan Tour event, which is an OWGR-sanctioned circuit.

The PGA Professional ended just six strokes off the lead at the Fairmont St Andrews Classic, where a certain Michael Stewart missed the cut. Stewart then finished T4th at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship on the DP World Tour just a month later.

Finch reached Final Qualifying for the Open Championship, after winning his regional event, last year. Also in 2025, he made the cut at the Asian Development Tour's Egyptian Open, and he has had plenty of high level experience from competing in the Q at Myrtle Beach in recent years.

Making the cut might look unlikely, but it's certainly not a foregone conclusion that he will just turn up and go home early. His invite undoubtedly adds intrigue to an event that is crying out for some extra attention, and I will be one of many cheering him on to make the weekend.

And finally, Finch is hardly taking the spot of a pro who has earned their way into the field.

The Mauritius Open is not the best-supported event of the season by any means, with almost all of the tour's top players skipping it. Last year, 11 sponsor's invitations were handed out and Finch will be one of these in 2026.

Sponsor's invites are undoubtedly controversial, but when there are so many up for grabs it seems harsh to be critical when one is given to someone who will genuinely adds to the TV and digital numbers.

What do you make of Finch's sponsor's invite? Let us know your view in the comments section. And will he make the cut? Find out on golfmonthly.com next month.

title: David Puig eyeing Ryder Cup spot at Adare Manor
article_text:
It seems that most pre-tournament press conferences this season will feature a European golfer declaring his Ryder Cup ambitions with Spain’s David Puig becoming the latest to eye up a spot at Adare Manor in September.

Puig is playing his first full campaign on the DP World Tour after plying the majority of his trade on LIV Golf. His big goal for the season is to become the twelfth Spaniard to play for Europe in the Ryder Cup, joining the likes of Sergio Garcia, Jon Rahm, Jose Maria Olazabal and Seve Ballesteros in the record books.

Speaking ahead of his title defence at the DP World Tour’s season opening BMW Australian PGA Championship, Puig, who reached a career high 56th in the world rankings last year, hopes to catch Luke Donald’s eye.

“It’s really important. It’s another dream of mine since I was young,” said Puig, who played at the Junior Ryder Cup in France in 2018.

“Playing in a Ryder Cup would be amazing. I’ll try my best. Hopefully it’s enough to be on the team in September.

“But it starts in weeks like this where playing good golf, it definitely matters. So it’s getting closer and closer and yeah, I’ll try my best and hopefully I’m part of the team in September.”

By winning the Joe Kirkwood Cup last year, Puig became just the second Spanish winner of the long-standing tournament after Ballesteros – a piece of history that the 24-year-old cherishes.

“Golfers, we don’t really get many victories throughout our careers, so, I definitely enjoyed that one, especially being my first – it’s something that I will remember forever,” he said.

The 24-year-old has been widely tipped as the next star of Spanish golf and he is part of a talented bunch coming through in Eugenio Chacarra, Angel Ayora and Jose Luis Ballester. He is relishing the prospect of playing a global campaign on the DP World Tour.

“I’ve been looking forward to playing on the DP World Tour since I was a little kid.

“Having a full year here, it’s a dream come true and I’m really looking forward to playing pretty much every week and getting to know all the European courses, Asia, Africa, Australia, and pretty much the whole schedule.

“It’s definitely something that I’ve been, again, dreaming since I was really young and I’ve got the chance of doing it this season.”

title: DP World Tour hands out another shock invite
article_text:
YouTube golf star Peter Finch has been offered a surprise chance to make his DP World Tour debut next month.

Finch, who boasts over 850,000 subscribers, has announced he has accepted a sponsor’s invite into the AfrAsia Bank Mauritius Open.

The England-based content creator is currently undergoing a challenge to break into the top 1,000 in the Official World Golf Rankings, but has never before been handed an opportunity of this magnitude.

“I’m thrilled to share that I will be teeing it up at the AfrAsia Bank Mauritius Open on the DP World Tour,” Finch wrote on Instagram.

“I cannot wait to get out to Mauritius and compete against some of the best players in the world!”

Last year, Finch made the cut and tied for 50th at the Egyptian Open, an Asian Development Tour event, which boosted his ranking.

He has also made Final Qualifying for The Open, as well as finishing T6 at the Fairmont St Andrews Classic on the Tartan Pro Tour earlier this year. But this is a level above, with the $1.5 million event headlined by two-time Masters champion Bubba Watson.

Multiple DP World Tour winners Casey Jarvis, Branden Grace, Thriston Lawrence and Dean Burmester are also set to tee it up in Mauritius.

Finch added: “I remember watching this tournament over the years and just thinking what an amazing spectacle and an amazing privilege it would be to play at these courses and that’s what we’re going to be doing.”

Finch confirmed he will be filming content at the 72-hole stroke play event, which begins on December 10.

title: Rick Shiels hits back after brutal dig from LIV Golf executive
article_text:
Rick Shiels has laughed off some brutal criticism aimed towards him during LIV Golf’s bankruptcy court proceedings after the league’s collapse.

The YouTube star, who boasts over three million subscribers and participated in this year’s $4million Internet Invitational, is one of the creditors owed money following LIV’s demise.

Shiels signed a strategic partnership with LIV at the start of 2025, promoting the league’s events as an official ambassador by filming videos with players at tournament venues.

But when the Saudi Public Investment Fund withdrew its funding from LIV at the end of this season, several of the league’s highest paid employees had not been paid the totality of their original contracts.

And it emerged in court documents that England-based Shiels was owed $1.4 million on his multi-year-deal. When asked why Shiels was owed that sum, LIV’s Chief Restructuring Officer David Orlofsky offered a cutting response.

“As I understand it, Rick Shiels is some sort of golf influencer, but I have never heard of him,” Orlofsky said. “So I couldn’t tell you much about him, but apparently his job was to write stuff and publicize stuff about the events.

“And because he has supposedly a following, people were supposed to – there’s supposed to be some value he added there. I couldn’t pick him out of a lineup.”

Responding to this quote later on Instagram, Shiels wrote, “Unbelievable” alongside a laughing face emoji. “David who?” he added.

In an exclusive interview with TG last year, Shiels explained his reasons for joining LIV, two years after conversations initially started with the breakaway league. He said that the opportunity to travel the world, bolster his team and have access to players like Jon Rahm and Brooks Koepka ultimately became irresistible.

But Shiels is not the only one who is now owed money after the LIV taps were turned off. While players were the biggest creditors, several small UK businesses have taken a hit after being left unpaid from the doomed $5 billion project.

According to invoices seen by the BBC, Global Infusion Group, a catering company in Buckinghamshire, near London, is owed roughly $420,000. BD365 Clean, a Suffolk-based cleaning agency, is owed just shy of $100,000. The company’s owner Krissi Foskett described the unpaid bills as “sickening”.

“How can they sleep at night,” Foskett told the BBC, “knowing they are potentially putting companies out of business?”

Meanwhile, Goodysphere, a family-run business that provides a sensory bus designed to help autistic children that might find events overwhelming, is still owed around $4,000.

title: What's new on the 2027 Race to Dubai?
article_text:
There will be a feel of all new but also familiar as we head through the Race to Dubai in 2027.

There are three events on the schedule that did not feature in 2026 as the historic national opens of Singapore, Portugal and Hong Kong return, all bringing returning venues with them.

Of the six venues that are new for 2027, we will be visiting two for the very first time, while as always, we will welcome a host of new stars to golf's global Tour.

Here, we take a look at a few of the events, venues and players to keep an eye out for in 2027.

While the three events added may not be new, far from it in some cases, they make a very welcome return across the Asian Swing, European Swing and Back 9.

Straight after the year's first Major Championship at the Masters Tournament we head to Sentosa Golf Club for the Deutsche Bank Singapore Open.

While the DP World Tour has been a regular visitor to Singapore since the early 90s and was there as recently as 2025, the Singapore Open has not been part of the schedule since 2012, when Matteo Manassero lifted the trophy.

Ian Poulter, three-time champion Adam Scott and Gonzalo Fernandez-Castaño also won the event on the DP World Tour, joining a roll of honour that includes Major champions Sergio Garcia and Shaun Micheel.

The European Swing then brings the return of the Open de Portugal | Cascais Lisboa for the first time since Garrick Higgo lifted the trophy in 2020.

The event was on the schedule every season barring two from 1973 to 2010 and had a list of winners including Sam Torrance, Colin Montgomerie, Miguel Ángel Jiménez, Thomas Bjørn and notably Pablo Martin as an amateur in 2007.

It returned in 2017 when Matt Wallace took the title and has since been a regular feature on the HotelPlanner Tour.

Our third returnee is one of the most storied events in golf as we head back east for the Hong Kong Open.

One of Asia’s most historic tournaments, it returns to the DP World Tour’s schedule for the first time since the 2019 season.

Established in 1959, the event was co-sanctioned by the DP World Tour and Asian Tour 18 times in total after first featuring on the DP World Tour’s schedule in 2002 and was last won as a DP World Tour event by Aaron Rai.

He is the fifth Major winner to lift the trophy in the DP World Tour era along with José María Olazábal, Pádraig Harrington, Rory McIlroy and Justin Rose and they join the likes of four-time winner Jiménez, Montgomerie and Poulter on the roll of honour.

Our return to Singapore also sees us back at Sentosa Golf Club, home of the four previous DP World Tour editions of the Singapore Open.

Designed by Ron Fream and opened in 1982, The Serapong Course sits on Sentosa Island and having undergone renovations, will present a different test to our last visit 14 years ago.

The Estrella Damm Catalunya Championship then brings a brand new venue as Empordà Golf hosts the second edition of the Spanish event.

A three-time venue on the HotelPlanner Tour across 2021 and 2022, Empordà's Dunes Course designed by Robert von Hagge has been evolving since its inception in 1989 and will provide a links-style test just back from the coast.

A returning venue is Oitavos Dunes Links Golf which will host the Open de Portugal on the DP World Tour for the fifth time the following week.

Opened in 2001, the Arthur Hills designed layout plays along the Atlantic coast and its links style produced wins for Paul Broadhurst in 2005, Pablo Martin in 2007, Grégory Bourdy in 2008 and Michael Hoey in 2009.

The next week we have our second entirely new venue of the season as PGA Frisco plays host to the year's second Major, the US PGA Championship.

Only opened in 2023 and designed by the renowned Gil Hanse, the rugged Fields Ranch East layout is set to host a number of PGA of America Championships over the coming years, with the body having its headquarters onsite.

From a brand new venue to a returning classic as Kennemer Golf and Country Club hosts the KLM Open for the first time since 2015.

In its current location since 1927, Kennemer's 18 holes used for the KLM Open are made up of holes from three separate nine-hole courses with some designed by Harry Colt and others by Frank Pennink.

Its 22 editions so far, 12 on the DP World Tour, have seen Seve Ballesteros claim his maiden victory and wins for the likes of Bobby Locke, Flory Van Docke, José María Olazábal, Darren Clarke and home hero Joost Luiten.

Towards the end of the Back 9 we then head east again to Hong Kong Golf Club and one of the most prestigious venues in Asian golf.

The event has been staged at the club ever since its inaugural edition in 1959 and is now played over a composite of the New and Eden courses.

The club can trace its history back to 1889 and has been in Fanling since 1911 when the Old Course opened, with the New (1931) and Eden (1969) following after.

The pathways to the DP World Tour always provide us with a plethora of new talent and 2027 will be no different as HotelPlanner Tour graduates, Qualifying School graduates and players from our partner tours around the world get their first taste of full-time membership.

title: History was within Nelly Korda’s grasp. 5 rounds kept her from grabbing it
article_text:
When the ink is dry on the obituary for Nelly Korda’s 2026 season, the top line will be about her blistering start, her mindset shift after a winless 2025 and her two major victories, including a dramatic U.S. Women’s Open win at Riviera.

Korda was fantastic to start the season. She set the golf world on fire and embraced her role as the main character in growing the sport. She achieved a lifelong dream by becoming a U.S. Women’s Open champion, won her second Chevron Championship and put herself one point away from reaching the LPGA Hall of Fame.

It was a historic season for Korda. But it was one that ended on Sunday with a third-place finish at the CME Group Tour Championship and Korda still being one point shy of etching her name into LPGA immortality. Despite fighting a two-way miss this week at Tiburon Golf Club, Korda put herself in position to win on Sunday and open history’s gates. She has said that she only focuses on the next shot. That she is driven by a love of competition and not the big-picture rewards that come her way when she plays “Nelly Golf.” But Korda admitted on Saturday in Naples that she has at times battled with blocking out the noise. She hears it and knows what’s at stake. At times, she has let that impact her game. But she knows what will bring her to her ultimate goal is her ability to keep what lies on the horizon from affecting how she does business.

“I would say that like obviously I’ve struggled with it, too,” Korda said on Saturday. “I understand everyone wants a story, but for me, I just love the game. Sometimes I struggle with it where I like listen to the outside, and I put a little bit more pressure on myself, but I feel like I’ve learned. I’ve had the same team through the majority of my career, pretty much my entire career, where they know how to pull me out of, you know — pull my head out of my ass, pretty much.

“I’m so grateful for them because we’re all human beings, right? We all kind of make mistakes. We all want to be perfect but we’re not. So tomorrow I’m just going to go [out] and have fun.”

title: Jeeno Thitikul surpasses Annika Sorenstam to become LPGA’s all-time money leader
article_text:
Jeeno Thitikul overcame both Nelly Korda and Annika Sorenstam Sunday at the CME Group Tour Championship.

Thitikul beat Korda head-to-head in the LPGA’s season finale, earning another $4 million in official earnings. That jumped her past Sorenstam on the tour’s all-time money list.

The 23-year-old Thai broke the stranglehold that the legendary Swede had atop career earnings since 2001.

Korda, for her part, finished solo third in Naples, Florida, and collected $550,000 to also move past Sorenstam.

Thitikul has won $12 million with her three consecutive wins in the season finale. In a sign of the times, this was her 12th victory on tour – compared to 72 for Sorenstam.

title: Lucas Herbert was ‘sick of the soap opera’ around LIV Golf. But this is what he loved
article_text:
Lucas Herbert says he was “sick of the soap opera” surrounding LIV Golf before its spectacular collapse, but insists the breakaway league transformed his game and has left him better equipped than ever to win a major championship.

The Victorian will tee it up at the Australian PGA Championship at The Lakes in Sydney on Thursday alongside fellow Australian stars Min Woo Lee, Adam Scott, Cameron Smith, Elvis Smylie and Marc Leishman before next week’s Australian Open at Kingston Heath.

For Herbert, Smith, Smylie and Leishman, the next fortnight is about adjusting to life after LIV, which was liquidated earlier this month after five years.

Herbert has no regrets about joining the Saudi-backed competition but admits the constant speculation surrounding its future took a toll on players.

“I was just sick of all that noise and just wanted to get some space away from it,” Herbert told reporters in Sydney on Monday.

“If you can find me a LIV player from this past year who didn’t get sick of the soap opera drama around it, I’ll find you a liar right there. It was pretty taxing. Some of it was fair opinion, some of it was crap, but it takes a toll on you.

“It became not even about whether our league was good. It became about whether it was even going to survive and whether we were going to have jobs and what we were going to do. We were still actively trying to make the league work … and produce a product to take in next year, and we were being asked, ‘What are you going to do next year?’

“No one outside the league made it easy for us. We had plenty of critics. I don’t think you can let the ending skew the whole view of everything that happened.”

As many of LIV’s biggest names confront the prospect of having to qualify for other tours, Herbert will return to the DP World (European) Tour in 2027, with the ambition of regaining his American PGA Tour card the following year.

Meanwhile, Smith has also secured a lifeline, agreeing to play a limited number of DP World Tour events in 2027 through a special invitation arrangement that falls short of full playing rights.

Herbert is among the favourites this week in Sydney after finishing tied for sixth at this year’s Open Championship at Royal Birkdale, where he equalled the major championship record with a second-round 62, narrowly missing a short putt on the final hole for an outright record.

The winner of that tournament, New Zealand’s Ryan Fox, will be chasing another piece of history next week when he attempts to become the first Kiwi to win the Australian Open, in a field headlined by world No.2 Rory McIlroy.

This is the first time the PGA Championship has been held in Sydney since 1998, with Queensland having long been the tournament’s traditional home.

“I’d love to at least win one [of the upcoming Australian tournaments] … to feel I’ve had the career that I’ve got the ability to have. I feel like I’m good enough to win these events,” Herbert said.

“I was also pretty grateful I got an opportunity to get somewhere to play next year. I would have understood if all of the tours told us to get lost.

“I want to go and get after it in the majors. What I did at [Royal] Birkdale this year was some of the most fun I’ve ever had on the golf course. A lot of people ask if I’m trying to get back to the PGA Tour. It would be great, but I also don’t really care that much if I’m consistently competing in the majors.”

While Smith, the 2022 Open champion, has struggled to recapture his best form since joining LIV, Herbert believes the lighter schedule and extended breaks between tournaments took his game to another level.

“We obviously made some great money - which you everyone wants to highlight pretty quickly - but we got incredible opportunities. My game got infinitely better as a result of going to LIV,” Herbert said. “I think I’ve never been in a better position to be able to contend and win a major championship. I don’t know that I would have got that opportunity had I not gone to LIV.”

Leishman, 43, is also approaching the Australian summer with renewed purpose, describing the next two tournaments as “pretty significant” opportunities to potentially secure a place at the Masters or the 2027 Open Championship at St Andrews.

The former world No.12 is undecided about returning to the grind of qualifying for the DP World Tour, but knows victory in either Sydney or Melbourne would secure status for two years.

Like Herbert, Leishman has no regrets about his decision to join LIV in 2022.

“I made a decision four and a half years ago to go over there and if I had that decision again, knowing what I know now, I would have done exactly the same thing,” Leishman said. “These last four years have definitely been the best four years of my life. I’m as happy now as I’ve ever been.”

title: Aussie has ‘no regrets’ about LIV Golf move despite career limbo
article_text:
Marc Leishman knows he has a big career call on his hands, but he has “no regrets” about his time playing on the now collapsed LIV Golf tour.

The careers of a number of star players were left in limbo due to the demise of the breakaway tour, with nine players, including fellow Australian star Cameron Smith, securing lifelines with the DP World Tour.

Smith put pen to paper on an agreement to play a number of invitational events next season with the DP World Tour, but Leishman has yet to formally announce whether he will do a similar deal.

Leishman, who first signed on with LIV Golf in August 2022, can secure his status on the DP World Tour over the next two weeks if he wins either the Australian PGA Championship or the Australian Open.

The 43-year-old has never won either tournament.

“These two weeks are definitely pretty significant to me,” Leishman told reporters at The Lakes in Sydney on Monday morning.

“I’m not too sure what the future holds for me at the moment. Obviously, it’s a little uncertain what the future holds for me, but if I knew exactly what was going to happen, I would have made the same decision.

“I’ve certainly got no regrets. I’m thankful for what (LIV) has given me.

“I’ve got a few things on the cards outside of golf, but being a competitor, I definitely want to stay really sharp on the course and keep playing.

“Where that is, I’m not sure yet, but I’m definitely motivated to try and play well here and to try and get myself some status on the DP World Tour.

If Leishman does not win over the next two weeks, he will have to look in a different direction.

One option for Leishman is to win the PGA Tour of Australasia’s Order of Merit, just as Travis Smyth did last season, to secure his DP World Tour membership.

He has already locked himself in to defend his title at the Victorian PGA Championship next month and also the mixed-gender Players Series in January.

While Leishman is open to doing whatever it takes to secure his status, he knows he has no interest in being away from his family for more than six months.

“I feel like I am past that grind,” he added.

“I don’t know if I am motivated to (play a full schedule). I certainly want to keep competing above that part of golf, testing yourself under pressure.

"You never say never, I'll play where I have to play to get status back."

If still unsuccessful, Leishman can fall back on his interest in golf course design. He has already begun a project of the kind close to his family home in Virginia in the United States, but he is interested in exploring opportunities in Victoria too.

The Australian PGA Championship will be held in Sydney from Thursday to Sunday and will be broadcast live on Nine and 9Now.

title: The PGA Tour season will end without fans. Davis Love III defended the controversial decision
article_text:
A lot will be on the line on Monday at Sea Island Resort when the 2026 PGA Tour season concludes. Players will be fighting to keep their PGA Tour cards, jump into the AON Next 10 or trying to secure the first win of their PGA Tour career.

But no one will be there to see the RSM Classic finish.

After Saturday’s third round was washed out by rain, the tournament announced it would finish on Monday, but no fans would be allowed on the ground. Fans with Sunday tickets were allowed to watch the golf on Sunday, but Saturday tickets were not honored and fans were asked to see the refund policy since no crowds will be allowed on Monday.

On Sunday, tournament host Davis Love III went on Golf Channel to discuss the decision to have a Monday finish with no fans. He said it was “disappointing” that a round with so much at stake would have no fanfare but said the tournament didn’t have enough volunteers to staff the event for an extra day.

“We’re going to have the last day of the PGA Tour of the year. We’ve got guys playing for not only winning a golf tournament but trying to improve their position, get a card for next year, and we can’t have fans because we’ve lost so many assets for tomorrow,” Love said. “Parking, mainly our 1,200 volunteers. That’s the biggest thing is we can’t safely have thousands of people out here unless we have the volunteers. Unfortunately, we are a small tournament that has a lot of great assets to it, but it also is challenging for us to round up enough people to safely — whether it’s security, whether it’s buses, whether it’s food, all those things — because of the weather, we can’t handle it tomorrow.

“So we’re going to be able to get the players to play, and that’s the main thing: give them a good golf course. Obviously, they won’t hear quite as much cheering. There will be a lot of people on 18, maybe, but it will be a quiet day and a special day. But it’s been disappointing. This is a community event. Our community pours themselves into this for weeks and weeks and weeks, and we just can’t really get enough support for tomorrow to get a whole lot of fans out here, and that’s disappointing.”

Love said he and the tournament will work to make things right with fans who bought Saturday tickets and couldn’t attend because of the Saturday washout and the decision to limit Sunday’s gallery to those with Sunday tickets. What that looks like is still undetermined.

“The technology of these tickets is challenging,” Love said about trying to change the day on the Saturday tickets. “Now there’s no paper tickets to hand out. It’s all done by computer. We will figure out a way between now and next year to accommodate what happened on Saturday. Our community does so much for us, we want to continue to do for our community. But this is ultimately about a local tournament, local support, raising money for charity and we want to continue that, and everybody that’s helped us, we’re going to continue to help them going forward. We’re just bummed that so many people didn’t get to see a finish today.”

Monday will see Michael Thorbjornsen and Rasmus Hojgaard arrive tied for the lead at 13 under, with Max Greyserman one shot off the pace. Thorbjornsen is gunning for his second win of the season, while Hojgaard needs to finish at least in a three-way tie for third to jump inside the top 100 and keep his PGA Tour card. They’ll battle on Monday with no gallery. Just them, their ball and an 18-hole walk.

“I’m just going to stay focused on what I want to do,” Thorbjornsen said of playing without a crowd. “I don’t think it makes any difference to me whether someone’s watching my ball flight or not. Hopefully the course is in good condition, hopefully the weather’s going to be a little better, so excited for that.”

The PGA Tour season will end on a fanless Monday in Sea Island. It will be an odd sight and not one the PGA Tour wants. But the stakes will be the same even if very few people are there to witness the outcome.

title: Smyth's 'bigger stage' finally beckons after LIV stint, eight-month wait
article_text:
Travis Smyth made LIV history in his short stint with the embattled tour in 2026 and with LIV gone and a DP World Tour card in hand, he's ready to start his full-time career on the "bigger stage" he's always wanted.

- Travis Smyth is making his first start as a fully-fledged DP World Tour member at the Australian PGA Championship after topping the Challenger PGA Tour of Australasia Order of Merit.

- Smyth, who earned well over $6 million from his stint with LIV Golf, admits disappointment that the breakaway circuit's liquidation has removed it from the golf "ecosystem".

- The 31-year-old faces one of his toughest fields in some time at The Lakes, lining up against DP World Tour regulars including Cam Smith, Lucas Herbert and David Puig.

Smyth was still weighing up whether he’d be part of LIV 2.0 when the plug was finally pulled on the breakaway circuit, adamant it could have been a part of the golf “ecosystem”.

But with a DP World Tour card locked and loaded Smyth, who collected well over $6 million from his in and out time with LIV, is re-focused on taking full advantage of his status starting with the Australian PGA Championship in Sydney this week.

Smyth, 31, is making his first ever start as a fully-fledged DP World Tour at The Lakes having secured playing rights through his victory in the 2025/26 Challenger PGA Tour of Australasia Order of Merit.

It’s the perfect launching pad for the New South Welshman, albeit some eight months after he secured his playing rights at the end of the last Australian season.

Smyth, now ranked 196th in the world, used that time to compete at significant events, winning the International Series Japan in April and playing in his second Open Championship at Royal Birkdale.

But he also played in six LIV Golf events, filling in on the all-Australian Ripper GC team for injured Elvis Smylie.

Mixed reports about LIV’s operation towards the end of its impactful five years have painted a picture of some dysfunction amid uncertainty but Smyth enjoyed the operation and its desire to take golf around the world.

With liquidation looming for LIV, Smyth said he had to feel a tinge of disappointment that another playing option for those like him, who operate on the fringes of the big tours, had disappeared.

“I'm a bit disappointed. All the talk from the players was that it was going to happen in some capacity and I was looking forward to seeing what was going to transpire from it,” he said after arriving at The Lakes.

“I wasn't quite sure 100% if I was going to play, but in the back of my mind it was definitely a strong decision. And I would have liked it, whether I played it or not, I still would have liked that LIV was still somewhat in the ecosystem of golf.

“I think what they're doing is really good. Going around the world, playing in these places that haven't had these sort of star players and me being a player at some of them and seeing firsthand the impact that we have on those areas was special.”

Smyth hits the PGA Championship off finishing 12th in the Philippines Open having played a run of Asian events knowing a “bigger stage” awaited.

“I still I love the Asian Tour, and I love travelling around that part of the world. But I always saw myself that when I play well, I feel like I can compete on a bigger stage and I've just always wanted that opportunity,” he said.

“Now with the help of the Aussie tour and winning that Order of Merit, it's catapulted me into the DP World Tour, and I just can't wait to tee it up. The weeks that I do play well, I can't wait to see where I stand with the rest of the crowd.”

The field at the PGA looms as arguably the toughest Smyth has encountered in some time, with a horde of the payers he’ll encounter weekly on the DP World Tour, including LIV evacuees Cam Smith, Lucas Herbert and reigning champion, Spain’s David Puig.

Smyth said the PGA and next week’s Australian Open always sit prominently on the calendar for Australian players but had to be approached as per any other tournament, for fear of getting lost in expectation or hope of joining some of the greatest names in golf to win both tournaments.

“There's always events that are heightened and I feel like I've done it long enough now, you just kind of have to accept that there are weeks that are going to be tougher than others mentally for different reasons,” he said.

“And sometimes you play well, sometimes you don't. Sometimes you really embrace the pressure, and it makes you play better. And then sometimes it gets the better of you and you play worse.

“So, whatever comes, I'm going to enjoy it and just give it the best.”

title: JJ Spaun Claims Third Title Of 2026 With Eight-Shot Victory In Japan
article_text:
While PGA Tour players battle to secure their futures at the RSM Classic in Sea Island, Georgia, one of the circuit's biggest names has been competing on the other side of the world.

JJ Spaun has no such concerns over his PGA Tour card, and instead opted to play in the Japan Golf Tour's Dunlop Phoenix Tournament.

It proved an inspired choice for the 2025 US Open champion, too, as he stormed to an eight-shot victory at Phoenix Country Club in Miyazaki.

The American carded rounds of 66, 70, 62 and 66 to finish on 16-under, with Japanese players Yusaku Hosono and Ryo Katsumata his closest challengers.

It was Spaun's first victory on the Japan Golf Tour and continued his excellent form, with the event marking his first start since his win at the DP World Tour's flagship event, the BMW PGA Championship in September.

Not only that, but it’s his third title in a brilliant season, after he claimed his second Valero Texas Open title on the PGA Tour in April.

Spaun was far from the only big name teeing it up in Japan. Ryo Ishikawa, who has 20 wins on the Japan Golf Tour, placed T4, while Japan’s biggest star, 2014 champion Hideki Matsuyama, finished in a tie for 14th.

Subscribe to the Golf Monthly newsletter to stay up to date with all the latest tour news, equipment news, reviews, head-to-heads and buyer’s guides from our team of experienced experts.

One shot ahead of Matsuyama was former LIV Golf player Michael La Sasso, who finished on three-under.

The American is set to make several DP World Tour appearances in 2027 after receiving tournament invitations despite missing out on a full card at Q-School.

PGA Tour winner Aldrich Potgieter also played, finishing T35 on two-over, while DP World Tour player Maximilian Steinlechner placed T41 on three-over.

Spaun joins an illustrious list of former Dunlop Phoenix Tournament champions, including Matsutama, Tiger Woods, Brooks Koepka, Luke Donald, Padraig Harrington, Thomas Bjorn, Tom Watson, Ernie Els and Seve Ballesteros.

Mike has over 25 years of experience in journalism, including writing on a range of sports throughout that time, such as golf, football and cricket. Now a freelance staff writer for Golf Monthly, he is dedicated to covering the game's most newsworthy stories.

He has written hundreds of articles on the game, from features offering insights into how members of the public can play some of the world's most revered courses, to breaking news stories affecting everything from the PGA Tour and LIV Golf to developmental Tours and the amateur game.

Mike grew up in East Yorkshire and began his career in journalism in 1997. He then moved to London in 2003 as his career flourished, and nowadays resides in New Brunswick, Canada, where he and his wife raise their young family less than a mile from his local course.

Kevin Cook’s acclaimed 2007 biography, Tommy’s Honour, about golf’s founding father and son, remains one of his all-time favourite sports books.

title: LPGA Tour: Jeeno Thitikul wins CME Group Tour Championship again and overtakes Annika Sorenstam's career money record
article_text:
Jeeno Thitikul has won the LPGA Tour's season-ending CME Group Tour Championship for a third consecutive year after storming to a two-shot victory in Florida.

Thitikul carded an eagle and five birdies during an impressive seven-under 65, pulling her clear of a congested leaderboard at Tiburon Golf Club and securing a 12th LPGA Tour title.

She finished on 24 under and two clear of Aki Iwai, who raced into contention with six birdies in the first 10 holes of her final-round 65, while world No 1 Nelly Korda finished in third spot.

Thitikul becomes the first player to win an LPGA Tour event three years running since Inbee Park at the KPMG Women's PGA Championship from 2013-2015, with her latest a fifth of another memorable season.

A $4m (£3.06m) first prize also sees her end Annika Sorenstam's 25-year stint at the top of the LPGA Tour's career money list, moving ahead of the Swede with a total of $24,292,858 (£20.3m).

Thitikul started the final day a shot behind A Lim Kim but made the dream start with a 12-foot eagle at the par-five first, then added a long-range birdie at the fourth and five-foot gain at the sixth to reach the turn in 32.

She started her back nine with a 10-foot birdie to edge back ahead of Iwai, who birdied six of her opening 10 holes in the group ahead and briefly levelled with another at the 13th, before Thitikul took advantage of the par-five 14th to reclaim top spot.

Iwai failed to capitalise on birdie opportunities over her closing holes as Thitikul doubled her lead with a two-putt birdie at the par-five 17th and closed out victory with a stress-free par at the last.

Korda also moved above Sorenstam's career-money record with her third-place finish, although extended her wait for the victory required to enter the LPGA Tour Hall of Fame.

"Still being able to compete when I didn't even really feel like I really had my trust in like a B or C game," Korda admitted. "So just proud of the way that I fought this week to kind of give myself a chance.

"It's really hard to go up against Jeeno [Thitikul] out here. I feel like she just has this place figured out. Maybe one day!"

Pajaree Anannarukarn, Yan Liu and Alison Lee shared fourth spot on 19 under, with overnight leader Kim in tied-seventh alongside Yuri Yoshida and Sei Young Kim after a final-round 72.

England's Lottie Woad jumped inside the top 20 with a final-round 67, while Charley Hull faded to a share of 23rd place after a one-over 73.

The WTGL season continues on Wednesday when Lottie Woad's Boston Common chase their first win of the campaign against Charley Hull's Atlanta Drive GC. Live coverage begins on Wednesday from 1am on Sky Sports Golf.

The 2027 LPGA Tour season begins with the Hilton Grand Vacations Tournament of Champions from February 4-7. Get the latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract.

title: Get to know DP World Tour Q-School graduates ahead of 2027 season opener
article_text:
Ben Coley takes a look at the 20 new DP World Tour members who came through Qualifying School, including some familiar faces and others we know less about.

What we know: Bombs it. As in, bombs it. Ranked the single best driver on the DP World Tour during his rookie season (excluding those with dual membership who played fewer rounds) so has been able to harness that power, but worse than 150th in all three of the other key SG categories. No wonder his best effort was in the Dunhill Links until he officially won Q-School via countback, those courses also good for his profile. Raw, then, and that explains run of good starts that amounted to nothing during spring and early summer. Mum Irish, dad Italian, to help explain name.

What we don't know: Whether he can make the necessary improvements to those shots the powerhouses often struggle with, like off-speed wedges and delicate chips. Also, whether or not the DP World Tour schedule will continue to work against players like him. In the Steyn City-Albatross-Dom Pedro-Marco Simone days there were ample opportunities for grip it and rip it golfers. Right now there are very few suitable courses.

What we know: Bombs it. As in, bombs it. That helped take him close to the very top of the amateur game (won the US Amateur) and explains inconsistencies as a professional. Looked to be finding that missing ingredient either side of last Christmas, a run triggered by winning the Saudi International, but was poor through summer and only scraped through Stage One before realising he was exempt for Final Stage. Bags of talent though and much more than an out-and-out bomber, for all he'll almost definitely rank inside the top 10 in driving distance. Not shy about where he goes to the loo.

What we don't know: Much about the rest of his game given absence of easily accessible LIV Golf statistics, although did rank ninth in strokes-gained approach in the Open Championship then third in the Dunhill Links. That bodes really well and is what helps separate him from compatriot Repetto Taylor. Same challenges apply when it comes to course suitability and it's a shame he probably won't get a game in the Dubai Desert Classic. Would be some irony if his schedule suffers for an influx of LIV players who didn't go and earn a card as he did.

What we know: That if you're a golf-loving parent from Australia, you'd do worse than choose the name 'Cameron' for your first-born son. This one won the Australian Boys' Amateur, succeeding DP World Tour winner Daniel Hillier, and won the Scottish Amateur the year after Marco Penge. He has pedigree in other words and it's started to show in the professional ranks as he finished second in last year's PGA Tour of Australia order of merit after taking his tally to four pro wins, generally in tough conditions. T28 in the Open was good, too.

What we don't know: Whether he can bridge the gap. Anthony Quayle couldn't capitalise on a strong start to the season and in general, we've seen a lack of emerging Australian talent since Min Woo Lee broke through. Michael Hollick (OK, a veteran South African not a young Australian) used the end-of-year Aussie events as a springboard to a shock DP World Tour win last year and we might get a good idea of what John has to offer this side of Christmas.

What we know: Also Spanish, also powerful, despite being quite small. Reached the top 10 in the World Amateur Golf Rankings so has to go down as a bit of an underachiever, but did look ready to win at DP World Tour level early in 2025 and received high praise from Tommy Fleetwood after they played together in the Dubai Desert Classic. Won't be easy out of a Q-School category and faces many of the same challenges as Repetto Taylor and Ballester, with the latter the one who ought to cope best.

What we don't know: If his driving figures from 2025 were an anomaly or a benchmark to return to. As with Repetto Taylor, the other three parts of his game are not up to scratch, but it's the downturn he's displayed off the tee this year which explains why he wound up back at Q-School, where a fourth-round 61 did much of the work. As with his compatriots, we also have to find out whether there are enough suitable courses these days.

What we know: That he's friends with Gareth Bale (caddied for him in a HotelPlanner Tour event), that he can still hit the whatsits out of the golf ball, and that his short-game is a big problem. It's 15 years since he burst on the scene as an amateur in the Open and the talent has always been there, but Lewis finished a lowly 89th on the HotelPlanner Tour standings in 2026 before finding a suitable set of courses at Final Stage, which he got into as a lucky loser. Still only 35, maybe there's still hope for him at a higher level.

What we don't know: Whether or not he's made any real progress around and on the greens. Chipping in particular has been a massive problem down the years and so has the putter, and these issues get harder to resolve with every passing year. We know how good he can be otherwise, that five-stroke win in the Korn Ferry Tour Championship and two wins in the Portugal Masters rather underlining a talent unfulfilled.

title: How Kevin Na has fared since leaving LIV Golf and reapplying for PGA Tour membership
article_text:
It was announced back in January that Kevin Na was leaving LIV Golf with his Iron Heads team set to be rebranded as Korean Golf Club for the 2026 season.

Na's departure was certainly a surprise. He had not been relegated at the end of the 2025 season. Nevertheless, his team decided to replace the 43-year-old, as Byeong Hun An made the jump from the PGA Tour to take over as captain.

Na applied to regain his PGA Tour membership shortly after his LIV exit. However, most of the players who left the breakaway league have had to serve a suspension of at least one year before they are able to return to their former circuit.

He has spent the majority of this season playing in Asia. Unfortunately, his form has not exactly forced the golfing world to sit up and take notice.

Despite being a five-time winner on the PGA Tour, Na never managed to contend for a victory on LIV. In fact, the South Korean-born golfer never finished inside the top-five at a LIV event.

You would have to go back to the 2024 season for his most recent top-10, which came in Hong Kong.

The 2026 season has been underwhelming, with his best finish in nine starts coming at the Philippine Open earlier this month. On that occasion, Na finished tied for 12th.

Elsewhere, he made three appearances on the DP World Tour. His best result was tied for 40th at the Austrian Alpine Open.

In total, he missed the cut on three occasions. Nevertheless, it seems that Na has his sights set on a return to the PGA Tour in the near future.

Na reportedly had his membership reinstated at a similar time to Brooks Koepka. And according to Eddie Pepperell, Na intends to return to the PGA Tour in January using a career money exemption.

Pepperell revealed Na's plans on The Chipping Forecast after playing alongside him in Austria back in May.

Obviously, there has been little talk of Na returning since then. And in truth, his results on the course do not exactly suggest that he is ready to be competitive at the highest level.

However, Na earned $37 million on the PGA Tour before leaving for LIV Golf in 2022. And at 43, he will hope that he can still spring a few surprises.

It will be very interesting to see if he ends up having a significant head-start on all of the players who have now moved on from LIV and are preparing to spend the upcoming season on the DP World Tour.

title: PGA Tour winner reveals 2027 plans after losing card
article_text:
Get the latest news, reviews, analysis and opinion, plus unmissable deals and exclusive offers. Please check the box of every email you wish to receive.

For the first time in more than a decade, Billy Horschel has lost his PGA Tour card. But it’s not all doom and gloom for the eight-time winner.

Horschel has held his card on the US-based circuit since 2013 but couldn’t salvage full playing rights for 2027 after missing the cut at the RSM Classic this weekend.

The 39-year-old entered the final event of the regular season at No.100 on the FedEx Cup standings, however, only the top 100 players secure cards for the following season. Albeit, Horschel will claim conditional status and, as it turns out, that means he still has plenty to look forward to.

Asked what difference finishing outside the top 100 will make to his schedule next year, he said: “Not much. I mean, listen, in 2023 I had a bad year, I was 125th. I had full status no matter what and I wasn’t in any Signature Events.

“[Then] I played really well, got in a couple of Signature Events. Didn’t take advantage of those Signature Events. But I look at 2023 and, going into 2024, I get to the Tour Championship without being guaranteed Signature Events.”

Despite losing his card, Horschel, who turned pro in 2009 and earned his PGA Tour card a year later, will get into almost every regular event on the circuit next season.

One he might require a sponsor’s exemption for, though, is the Waste Management Phoenix Open. Albeit, Horschel has a plan for that, too.

“I’m pretty much going to get in every open event on the PGA Tour,” he said, “but probably not Phoenix, I’m going to have to make a call to Chance Cosby [executive director of The Thunderbirds, the organisation that hosts the event], who I’ve had a relationship with at Ping for a long time.

“I think they get one or two sponsor exemptions and there’s going to be a lot of guys pushing for that, so that’s going to be a tough one.

“Then I haven’t looked at it too far in advance, but I know I’m going to get in quite a few events, and I’ve got to be able to take advantage of those opportunities like Ben Kohles did, Jackson Suber, Doug Ghim.

“Those guys did a really good job this year of taking advantage of it. You know, those three guys right there are great people to copy for next year.”

It was a brutal end to the season in Sea Island for Horschel, who finished the second-round bogey-bogey-double bogey to miss the cut.

Before the RSM Classic, he’d missed 12 cuts in 30 starts, recording only one top-ten finish. Assessing his season, Horschel gave it an F-plus.

“I gave myself plenty of opportunities out here,” he said. “I’ve played the most events of anyone on the PGA Tour of 31 events which, six months after hip surgery, you don’t think you’re going to play 31 events and you get through physically with no issues, it’s really cool.

“But at the same time, it sucks that I gave myself that many opportunities and I didn’t take advantage of all those opportunities to play well. I could rattle off the four or five events I missed cuts by a shot, or the events where I played well, I was in good position after 36 holes, and I just didn’t play well on the weekend. Everything I have historically done over my career; I did none of that this year so that’s a disappointing thing of it.”

title: Pro 'appalled' at tour's stance on ex-LIV players: 'Borderline unethical'
article_text:
Longtime DP World Tour pro Eddie Pepperell has been an outspoken critic of LIV Golf for years. But with the controversial league now defunct, Pepperell is focused on a different issue involving LIV.

In the weeks before and since LIV Golf began to wind down operations, several of its players have signed on with the DP World Tour for 2027.

While the roster of invites features stars like Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau, other less-accomplished LIV players have been welcomed back as well.

In Pepperell’s eyes, this is a big problem. Every spot given to a former LIV player next year could negatively impact players who stayed loyal to the DP World Tour amid pro golf’s civil war.

On the latest episode of “The Chipping Forecast” podcast, Pepperell called the DP World Tour’s decision to issue invites to a large group of ex-LIV players “pretty appalling” and declared that it had “massively affected” his feelings toward the tour.

Pepperell is a regular co-host of “The Chipping Forecast” podcast, along with Iain Carter and Andrew Cotter.

When the discussion in their most recent episode turned toward the recent LIV Golf news, and the DP World Tour’s actions in response to LIV’s end, Pepperell didn’t hold back.

He argued that former LIV Golf players are “being handed opportunities” on the DP World Tour despite playing for a league whose operators were openly trying to “destroy” the European circuit.

“Let’s not forget, because it’s so easy to forget given how quickly things can shift, these [players] are coming from a tour that, as [DP World Tour CEO] Guy Kinnings just described, was set to destroy our own. And yet they’re still being handed opportunities,” Pepperell said. “It’s not the same as just giving an invite to Rory McIlroy when he first came out, or another player who is an up-and-coming star but hasn’t participated in a league that had ulterior motives and a deleterious impact on the DP World Tour.”

Pepperell admitted that he’d been “grappling” with this issue for weeks, and he acknowledged that the DP World Tour’s leaders are in a difficult situation in light of LIV’s end.

Ultimately, though, he argued that the decision to invite so many former LIV pros back to the DP World Tour was “borderline unethical.”

“I’ve really been grappling with this, and it’s been a bit of a stressful two weeks in my mind, because it does start to bring in ethical considerations, because this is borderline unethical. You can have different views on the strategic, commercial things as you see it panning out,” Pepperell said.

Specifically, Pepperell’s ethical qualms can be found in the DP World Tour’s decision to prioritize some LIV players over DP World Tour players.

“I do think there’s also an ethical component to this and – and I want to show some restraint – but I’m pretty appalled and it has massively affected the way I feel towards the tour,” Pepperell said. “And I predicted that would happen when I wrote that Substack a few weeks ago, called Charles and Eddie, and it has happened.”

Pepperell is referring to a lengthy post he made on Substack weeks ago, in which he argued that, aside from the biggest stars, ex-LIV Golf players should be forced to qualify for the DP World Tour through Q-school.

“The Joaquin Niemanns of the world, Cam Smith, Bryson of course. Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton have their exemptions,” Pepperell wrote on Substack. “Truthfully from my perspective not much else needed to be done, just ensure everybody else goes back to the qualifying school. The idea that Charles Howell III is on this list, with all due respect to Charles – he’s a terrific guy – is utterly bizarre.”

Pepperell is a two-time DP World Tour winner, but he’s fallen on hard times in recent years. He battled through Q-school last season to earn his DP World Tour card for 2026. He finished this year’s Race to Dubai at 101st in the standings, just missing out on a full card for 2027.

title: ‘It Threw Off Our Order’: Davis Love III Reveals How LIV Golf Pros Disrupted Team USA's Ryder Cup Order
article_text:
A Ryder Cup captaincy is usually a queue. Names are pencilled in years ahead, future captains learn the job as assistants, and everyone knows who is next in line. Then LIV Golf walked in and started rubbing names off the list. That is how Davis Love III described the last few years on the Fully Equipped podcast. The former US captain explained how the Saudi-backed league unsettled Team USA's plans from the inside.

"But, you know, you've got to remember LIV Tour has had a huge impact. It wasn't a ripple effect. It was a bomb effect through all of golf. It threw off our order of captains. It left us not knowing if guys were going to be able to play or not. It obviously affected Europe more than us in terms of understanding who was going to get to play, but it threw us off our order. And then, obviously, Tiger threw us off the order a little bit as well," Love III said on the show.

Love then compared the shock to the one faced by the man running the PGA Tour at the time.

"So it's not unlike Jay Monahan. Jay Monahan, incredible commissioner. He didn't see COVID coming. He didn't see LIV Golf, the Saudis, coming. And nobody can predict that. You can predict economics, or you can predict weather a little bit, but you can't predict things like that. We're just golfers thrown into a captain's role."

The "order" Love describes is the unwritten pipeline that turns a Ryder Cup veteran into a captain. Europe felt the disruption particularly sharply. Henrik Stenson was named 2023 captain in March 2022 but was stripped of the job that July, hours before announcing he was joining LIV. Luke Donald took over. Five players from Europe's 2021 team later left for LIV, and three of its vice captains went with them.

The US captaincy pipeline was disrupted, too. Golf Digest reported in 2022 that Phil Mickelson was widely expected to serve as an assistant under Zach Johnson in 2023 before taking over as captain at Bethpage in 2025.

Instead, the US went into the 2022 Presidents Cup without Dustin Johnson, Bryson DeChambeau, or Patrick Reed, and Phil Mickelson was no longer in the picture as a potential vice captain.

Love had also warned players about the consequences of joining LIV. "We tried to tell these guys before they went to LIV," he told Sports Illustrated in 2023.

The other disruption Love mentioned was Tiger Woods. The PGA of America waited months for Woods to accept the 2025 captaincy, but he eventually turned it down. Keegan Bradley was named instead in July 2024, despite never having served as an assistant captain. Woods stepped aside again for 2027 after his arrest on suspicion of DUI, opening the door for Jim Furyk in April.

That is why Love speaks so warmly about Furyk. In his words, the PGA of America wanted "stability" and "organization" during a time of disarray. Furyk's record backs up the choice. He lost the 2018 Ryder Cup 17.5-10.5 in Paris, then led the US to victory at the 2024 Presidents Cup and served as a vice captain at Bethpage. He has since added Stewart Cink and Justin Leonard to his staff, with the Americans still chasing their first win in Europe since 1993. Love believes Furyk is "way ahead of where we were four or five Ryder Cups ago."

Love also explained what he believes a captain should and should not do, drawing on his own experience with the 2016 team at Hazeltine.

"Our job is to give them new clothes and a new bag, some messaging, and a positive attitude. Bob Rotella helped me with the Hazeltine Ryder Cup team. He said, 'Okay, guys, you've never played together before. You have no record. You're a new team, and you're the home team. Let's go show off.' So we went out, had fun, and showed off."

As for Furyk, Love pointed to the Europeans as an example to follow. Donald, who is chasing a third straight win, "has developed a system, and he's running it," Love said, adding that his team believes in it.

For now, the Ryder Cup remains much anticipated, and who steals the cup next year is yet to be seen.

title: 'I was scared': LPGA player confesses to lying about rules breach before DQ
article_text:
For Scarlett Schremmer, the 2026 ANNIKA event was supposed to be the start of a promising LPGA career. Instead, the University of Miami golfer was left “embarrassed” following a rules breach that resulted in her disqualification.

As if a college golfer getting DQ’d in her LPGA debut wasn’t bad enough, the story took a turn for the worse this week.

On Friday, Schremmer took to Instagram to deliver a surprising confession: she lied to LPGA rules officials when questioned about the rules breach that led to her DQ.

On Saturday at last week’s ANNIKA event, the LPGA announced that Schremmer had been disqualified for a rules breach. Schremmer’s offense was using a yardage book prohibited by a Model Local Rule in place at all LPGA Tour events.

Following her DQ, Schremmer broke her silence in a statement on Instagram, saying she “had a green reading yardage book in my bag this week that’s allowed in college golf but isn’t permitted on the LPGA Tour. That’s on me. I should have checked, and it’s a lesson learned.”

What she didn’t admit to was using the illegal yardage book during the tournament. But Golfweek’s Beth Ann Nichols later reported that LPGA rules officials had been alerted to Schremmer’s use of the illegal yardage book as early as Thursday’s first round. Those officials took no action until photo evidence of Schremmer’s offenses turned up on Saturday.

Nichols’ report also included one more detail that contradicted Schremmer’s initial statement. When questioned about the yardage book, Schremmer denied using it.

That changed on Friday, when Schremmer released a new statement on Instagram. This time, the college golfer admitted to wrongly telling rules officials that the illegal yardage book in her bag was “not in use.” Schremmer also apologized for her “extremely poor decision,” saying fear and embarrassment led her to lie.

“When I was approached about it, I was scared, embarrassed, and made an extremely poor decision in saying it was not in use,” Schremmer wrote on Instagram on Friday. “I deeply regret that, I always will, and I want to own that mistake.”

She continued by writing that golf had taught her about “integrity, accountability, and respect for the game,” and that her actions during the ANNIKA event “did not reflect those values or the person I strive to be.”

Schremmer also said that she hopes to rebuild her reputation “through actions rather than words” over time.

You can read Schremmer’s full Instagram statement below.

“Over the past few days, I’ve spent a lot of time reflecting on what happened last week and, more importantly, how I handled the situation. I had no idea that I had a yardage book with illegal information. When I was approached about it, I was scared, embarrassed, and made an extremely poor decision in saying it was not in use. I deeply regret that, I always will, and I want to own that mistake.

“Golf has taught me so much about integrity, accountability, and respect for the game. More than anything, I genuinely love playing golf, and I have always understood that being a competitor means respecting the game and the standards that come with it. I know that my actions and the way I handled this situation did not reflect those values or the person I strive to be. This experience has given me a lot to think about, both as a golfer and as a person. I understand that trust is earned through actions rather than words, and I know that rebuilding it takes time. I am committed to learning from this, growing through it, and demonstrating through my actions that I can move forward with greater honesty, maturity and accountability.”

LPGA all-time money list: Three active players closing in on Annika Sorenstam’s record

Annika Sorenstam’s grip on the LPGA Tour’s all-time money list is nearing an end.

Sorenstam’s 25-year record of $22,583,693 could finally be trumped on Sunday at the CME Group Tour Championship.
